Snow covers the Green Meadows and Green Forest, ice binds the Big River and Smiling Pool, and Blacky must use his eyes for all they are worth to find food. Burgess turns each scrape into a small lesson about curiosity and caution. Young readers get an animal tale that teaches woodland ways through one crow's misadventures.
51112-the-other-now:
Murray Leinster bends time in The Other Now, from the March 1951 issue of Galaxy Science Fiction. Phil Bard draws the plates. The tale opens on a flat contradiction: he knew his wife was dead, because he had seen her buried. But it was only one possibility out of infinitely many.

It was self evident nonsense, the narrator grants. If Jimmy Patterson had told anybody but Haynes, calm men in white jackets would have taken him away for treatment. The facts are patently impossible, but they are satisfying, the voice holds. Haynes would like very much to know exactly why it happened in the case of Jimmy and Jane, and nobody else. It began about three months after Jane was killed in a freak accident. Jimmy had taken her death hard, and coming home to an empty house galled him nightly.
51152-appointment-in-tomorrow:
Appointment in Tomorrow is a story by Fritz Leiber, from a magazine of science fiction dated July nineteen fifty one. Pictures by Ed Alexander go with it. A question heads the tale: can a world exist without moral values. Or does the lack of morality itself become a moral value, it asks.

The first rays of the sun touch a ruined America in the opening. They pierce the tops of Atlantic waves and light a rusty circle of steel skeletons in Manhattan. A brass plaque marks the martyrdom of three physicists after a great bomb. A girl sleeps off a drunk on a roof garden nearby. The sun strikes green fire from the glassy blot where old Washington stood. The tale surveys a land of mask fads, new blue laws, and an endless war.
5121-dark-hollow:
Anna Katharine Green's mystery opens with a woman in purple. A missing man named Bela may be living or dead, and nobody can settle which. From that puzzle, the story moves through veiled meetings, a house with a secret room, a courtroom. A door of mystery opens, as old family misfortunes come back to accuse the living.

Green, a pioneer of the American detective novel, builds suspense through documents, testimony, and slow revelation rather than chases. Readers who enjoy classic mysteries of manners will find a carefully plotted puzzle, with a strong sense of place and a heroine caught between loyalty and truth.
51740-don-t-look-now:
Leonard Rubin wrote Don’t Look Now, a wry tale of a sick rich man. Galaxy magazine ran the story in April nineteen hundred sixty. Ad men on motor skates open its strange future world scene. Hover craft bear the sick through bright white halls in it.

Miss Knox, a nurse, bars two ad men from the sick craft at the door. Their flat cases sprout coil wires, and their faces blur to sameness. Barger, the great man, comes down sun blind and mute with pain. His throat ill is the worst laryngitis she has yet seen. Dead ills come back fierce when loosed anew, the tale lets fall. Gesner, the land’s first throat man, bends fat and short to the bed. Brooks the ray man herds his class of young medics in the wake. A gold calf could not draw more stares than Gesner at work.
51982-simeon-tetlow-s-shadow:
Simeon Tetlows Shadow is a novel of rail life by Jennette Lee. The gift page sends the book to the authors own kin of the same name. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen hundred and nine. Its hero is the head of a great road of rails and stock cars.

Tetlow sits bent at his desk in dusk light as the tale opens at three. His young aide rises to switch on the lamps for the dim room. The road lines are likened to nerves in the thin frame of the old chief. Orders from his small room move loads of beasts and folk far off. Power, age, and the aide bond form the knot of the tale.
52138-motor-matt-s-engagement-or-on-the-:
Motor Matt's Engagement is one week's tale of a boy and his road craft. It is count twenty seven of a week sheet of such tales. It bears the date of a day in the eighth month of nineteen hundred and nine. Its price is five cents a copy. The house of the sheet is a great New York house of cheap tales. A plate at the front shows the hero at his craft.

In that plate the boy coaxes the last bit of speed from his craft. He shouts words of cheer to a dire scared girl on the high wire of a show. The parts of the tale start on the banks of a great stream. In the band tent, a man who hears in hid, and strange deeds come next.
52153-the-motor-boys-on-a-ranch-or-ned-b:
Clarence Young wrote The Motor Boys on a Ranch, or Ned, Bob and Jerry Among the Cowboys, copyrighted in 1917. A frontispiece shows raiders rushing to the attack with a fusillade of revolver shots. The series list runs to twenty-one volumes.

The Motor Boys had already travelled overland, in Mexico, across the plains, afloat, on the Atlantic and Pacific, in the clouds, and over the Rockies and the ocean. They had gone under the sea, after a fortune, on the border, and at Boxwood Hall. This time the three chums take their motors west to a ranch. Readers get a boys' series adventure trading roads for cowboys, with the machine-age heroes on horse country.
5231-the-way-we-live-now:
Anthony Trollope's great satire, published in monthly parts from 1874 to 1875. It takes aim at the speculation and fraud of its age. Its central figure is Augustus Melmotte, a financier of mysterious wealth who dazzles London society, promotes grand schemes. He seeks a place in Parliament, while families scheme for marriages and money around him.

Trollope follows dozens of characters, from aristocrats to clerks, showing how greed corrupts love, politics, and business alike. The novel stands as his longest and most ambitious work. It remains a brilliant portrait of a society learning to live on credit, rumour, and show.
52397-motor-matt-s-short-circuit-or-the-:
Motor Matt's Short Circuit, or The Mahout's Vow is number 28 of Motor Stories, a weekly issued by Street and Smith of New York on September 4, 1909. The five-cent story is credited to the author of Motor Matt. Its hero, Matt King, is called the king of the motor boys.

The tale opens at a circus, with a serpent charmer and a bad elephant. The cover picture shows the huge beast towering over Matt, who holds his ground. Chapters bring a robbery, a cobra in the air, and a meeting with a Hindu mahout. Matt's chums include Joe McGlory, a young cowboy, and Ping, a Chinese boy who works for him. The story mixes motors, circus danger, and mystery in the brisk dime-novel manner.
52608-for-his-country-and-grandmother-an:
Marshall Saunders wrote two tales in one small book, printed at Boston in 1900. His Beautiful Joe stands first in a list of his works at the front. Drawings by Louis Meynell and others fill the pages. The front picture, from a youth's magazine, shows a cry: mademoiselle, you are an American?

The first tale opens on a river bank in France. A weary lad sings of his country and breaks down mid song. A fat footman sleeps on the grass with a novel in hand. An old goat creeps up and eats the book leaf by leaf. The second tale treats a grandmother and a crow, in the same warm vein as the tales of animals that made Saunders famed.
52888-what-every-girl-should-know:
What Every Girl Should Know is a plain health book by Margaret Sanger. Sentinel Printing of Reading, Pennsylvania, put the small book out. Sanger had writ How Six Little Children Were Taught the Truth before. She gives the book with love to the working girls of the world. Seven chapters run from girlhood to the change of life at the end.

Chapters treat growth of body and mind in the girlhood years first. Puberty and its disorders get a full chapter in plain words. The sexual impulse in girls, beasts, and men fills the next part. Reproduction and the hygiene of pregnancy follow in due order then. A hard chapter names the fruits of ignorance and silence in youth. Two dread diseases stand named there with their causes laid bare. Sanger wrote to give girls facts that silence had kept from them.
532-at-the-foot-of-the-rainbow:
Gene Stratton-Porter sets this Wabash tale among rat catchers, coons, and a rainbow's promise. Dannie and Jimmy Malone, friends and rivals, trap, fish, and court Mary Malone through seasons of rain and sun. A kingfisher, a black bass, and a pot of gold at the rainbow's foot thread the chapters.

Stratton-Porter writes nature with loving care, from river banks to orchards. A life sketch of the author fronts the book, praising her Limberlost work. The novel reads as a gentle romance of country folk, where love, work, and the land itself point toward hope.
53415-poems-you-ought-to-know:
Elia W Peattie, literary editor of the Chicago Tribune, selects Poems You Ought to Know, copyrighted in 1902 and illustrated by Ellsworth Young. Her epigraph urges every busy reader to secure a few minutes daily for refreshment of the inner life with a bit of poetry. The contents run alphabetically by poet, from Joseph Addison's Spacious Firmament to psalms ascribed to David.

Familiar pieces include Elizabeth Akers Allen's Rock Me to Sleep, Bryant's Thanatopsis, Byron's She Walks in Beauty and Coleridge's Kubla Khan. Browning, Burns, Henley's Invictus, Holmes and dozens more fill out the anthology.
5349-castle-craneycrow:
George Barr McCutcheon's Castle Craneycrow, published in New York in 1902, opens with Philip Quentin lecturing his servant on mind over matter. He then cheerfully takes him by the throat and throws him into a far corner. The servant, half his master's size, answers with picturesque language, but his loyalty and faithfulness are beyond doubt.

Quentin's career, already colourful, carries him toward a castle, a mystery. Romance follows, in the Ruritanian manner McCutcheon made famous. Readers get a brisk adventure of the period, with a strong hero, a loyal servant. A plot moves from a servant's scolding to a castle's secrets.
54632-boy-scout-explorers-at-headless-ho:
Don Palmer wrote a tale of Boy Scout Explorers at Headless Hollow for young readers. Cupples and Leon Company held the rights in New York in 1957. Twenty-five chapters run from Old Stony to a final rendezvous. A plate shows two men in a fight high on cliffs.

Hap Livingston drives Explorer Post 21 home from Philmont Ranch in New Mexico. War Washburn, Willie Medaugh, Jack Hartwell, and Ken Dougherty ride with him. A treasure map, a ghost town, warm ashes, and an avalanche crowd the road. Scouts get a fast tale of camp craft, nerve, and teamwork.
56909-river-and-canal-engineering-the-ch:
Bellasis wrote River and Canal Engineering, a technical book printed in London in 1913, with seventy-two illustrations. Bellasis had served as superintending engineer in the irrigation branch of the Public Works Department of India. Earlier books by him treated hydraulics, Punjab rivers, and suction caused by ships.

The work sets out the traits of open flowing streams and the rules for dealing with them. Early chapters cover rainfall records, how rain is measured, and how forests affect runoff. Design and building of river and canal works follow in detail for working engineers. Students of water works get a clear, practice-based guide from long service in India.
57406-what-a-young-wife-ought-to-know:
Emma F Angell Drake wrote What a Young Wife Ought to Know, the thousand dollar prize book of its series. The Vir Publishing Company issued it at Philadelphia, London, and Toronto. The copyrights stand in Sylvanus Stall's name for 1901 and 1902. Drake took her medical degree at Boston University. She had been physician and principal of Mr Moody's school at Northfield. She also taught obstetrics at the Denver homeopathic medical school.

The book stands in the Pure Books on Avoided Subjects series. Stall wrote the volumes for boys, men, husbands, and men of forty-five. Mary Wood-Allen and Drake wrote those for girls, young women, wives, and women of forty-five. Each volume sold at a dollar in America and four shillings in Britain. Drake's book gave new wives plain medical counsel on marriage and maternity.
57662-it-s-your-fairy-tale-you-know:
It's Your Fairy Tale, You Know is a children's fantasy by Elizabeth Rhodes Jackson. Brimmer published it at Boston in 1922, with pictures by Kattelle. Jackson dedicates it to her three children by name. The contents begin with the wishing stone, then the pixie starts it, and the pixie's first task follows.

Wendell, the hero, finds an unexpected ally and meets a frog somewhat out of the common. The story of the enchanted maiden leads to Wendell working the midnight spell. Cousin Virginia has a caller, the charm breaks, and Wendell enters the giant's house. A cloak of darkness, blind man's buff with the giant, a cap of thought, and a magic book fill the later chapters. The tale opens in a children's library room, where Wendell reads on and on like a true bookworm. Jackson lets her hero step into the fairy world and shape the tale himself.
58294-trees-you-want-to-know:
Donald Peattie wrote Trees You Want to Know, in 1934. Whitman at Racine, Wisconsin, put out the field book. Eastern tree pictures come from a classic sylva of North America. Western trees were drawn by Taylor for this volume. Each tree gets the same treatment here.

Shape, bark, fruit, and range make each entry. California nutmeg stands pyramidal, round topped in age, it says. Fifteen to ninety feet tall, its olive-like fruit hides a seed. The flesh of that fruit is an aril round a pit, it notes. Its range is the coast ranges and the Sierra of California. A Florida yew, rare in the northwest of that state, follows. The Pacific yew bears a scarlet coat around its seed. Limber pine stands broadly round topped at forty feet and more. Peattie gives the common trees a pocket portrait each.
58301-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this guide to the Project Gutenberg texts of Harriet Beecher Stowe. The Index lists her works as the project holds them, with their tables of contents laid out for the reader. Uncle Tom's Cabin heads the list, as it must.

A young folks' edition of the Cabin and a picture book from it follow. Queer Little Folks and The American Woman's Home come next. A life of Stowe by her son stands here too. Pink and White Tyranny, Sunny Memories of Foreign Lands, and Oldtown Fireside Stories fill the shelf. The Pearl of Orr's Island, Palmetto-Leaves, and The Minister's Wooing round out a full map of her fame.
58784-and-gone-tomorrow:
And Gone Tomorrow is a science fiction story by Andy Offutt. It appeared in Worlds of If magazine in December 1954. The story won a thousand dollar prize in a college contest. That contest asked what life in America would be like in a century. Offutt was then an undergraduate at the University of Louisville. It was his first published story, as an amateur entry. 

The story pictures America in the year 2054. By then it is part of a world empire. An Italian dictator runs that empire, in the tale. Its ways echo the Caesars and the early Roman Empire. There is one language and one religion in that world. Customs and laws have changed to suit the times. But human nature has not changed, the note stresses. Faction clashes with faction as it always has. The piece is a period entry in a famous contest.
591-flame-and-shadow:
Sara Teasdale gathers lyrics of love, place, and war in this volume, arranged in twelve sections. Blue squills, stars, and meadowlarks open the book; St. Louis sunsets, Cuban gardens, and Santa Barbara springs follow. Later sections hold war poems, including the famed There Will Come Soft Rains, and quiet songs of loss.

Teasdale writes in short, clear lines, with images of sea, night, and season. Love here is tender and often fleeting, yet never bitter. The book marks Teasdale at her mature best, where plain music carries deep feeling without show.
59514-after-some-tomorrow:
After Some Tomorrow is a science fiction story by Mack Reynolds. It appeared in Worlds of If in June 1956. The scene is a world long after some great fall. Alan is the Wolf clan's only husband. He teaches the young people their myth-legend. Girls are bored by the tales, and boys hang open-mouthed. The telling has changed since his own boyhood, he notes. In his youth a sterility test still hung over him.

Old books speak of women at home with children. To say such things now would cross decency's bounds. His daughter Helen asks for tales of true fighting. Then shots ring out below the grove. Reynolds often built futures from odd social turns. A clan with one husband is such a turn. The tale asks what manhood means in that world.
5960-little-sister-snow:
Frances Little sets her tale in Japan, in a quaint old garden under early spring sun. Light loosens a tiny rivulet from winter's grip and speeds it toward a miniature lake where goldfish dart. Into this scene comes Yuki Chan, a child who takes a stray petal blown into her face as a challenge.

The illustrations promise prayer, paint and brush, tea service, and lonely hours, with old people and a father's summons in the background. Little writes for readers who enjoy a gentle, picture-filled story. The child's small acts of courage and devotion carry a tale of life in a Japanese household.
59800-picture-show:
Siegfried Sassoon gathered these poems in a volume printed at New York in 1920 and dedicated to John Masefield. Sassoon was already known for The Old Huntsman and Counter-Attack, and the war stands behind much of the book. The title poem watches faces flicker past like a picture-show, glad or grievous, gone in a moment's gesture. Life, it says, is just the picture dancing on a screen.

War poems come early: Reconciliation, written in November 1918, asks a mourner at a hero's grave to remember the German soldiers and the mothers of the men who killed his son. A concert party at an Egyptian base camp, a night on the convoy, and a dug-out follow. Later the book widens to portraits, songs, and quiet pieces, closing with Everyone Sang.
59864-the-silver-arrow:
The Silver Arrow is a tale tract by Elbert Hubbard, struck at his famed craft press in nineteen twenty-three. It opens with the tale of a court man who spread his cloak in the path of a great queen. That act won him her own grace, the tract says. The queen was past twenty years the mans more in age, in her fifth decade past his third.

Hubbard says the man did two great things, one for each of two lands. He taught one land the use of the leaf of smoke, and he found the root crop of the next in the new world. The queen fed his aims and praised his gifts with soft taps of love. Yet her spies dogged his steps past his will, and that watch put a chill on his warm heart. The tract turns on that bond.
59932-canada-to-day-and-to-morrow:
Canada To-Day and To-Morrow is a travel book by Arthur Copping, printed by Cassell in 1911. It carries six full page colour plates by Harold Copping and thirty four pictures in black and white. The book is dedicated to Frank Oliver, Canada's minister of the interior. Nineteen chapters take the reader across the Dominion, from Quebec province to British Columbia, with an index at the end.

The chapters cover the destiny of the Dominion and a look back at its past. They take in Quebec, Niagara and its water power, the lumber trade, and Toronto with its exhibition. Later chapters treat the new Hudson Bay route, the experiences of immigrants, and Winnipeg at its centenary. The colour plates show the Parliament Buildings at Ottawa, Quebec in winter, and the big trees of Vancouver.
6044-quill-s-window:
George Barr McCutcheon opens Quill's Window on a hot August day, as a young man and an old one sit in willow shade beside a wide, still river. Sun glare fails to pierce their shelter, while out on the slow river it beats down and raises a pale vapor that dazzles the eye.

Chapters promise a forbidden rock, a story the old man told, Courtney Thane, Dowd's tavern, trespass, and a face at the window. Rosabel appears, shadows gather, and a disappearance, a thrower of stones, and a message with its answer follow. McCutcheon builds a riverside mystery around an old trail and a window.
60742-wongo-and-the-wise-old-crow:
Grace and Carl Moon tell animal tales of a forest called Timbertangle in a children's book issued at Chicago in 1923. Carl Moon drew the pictures, and the book is given to two young listeners, Francis and Mary Caryl. An opening verse promises a quarrel, a plot, and a villain as bad as can be.

Wongo, a small brown bear, wakes in his cave at dawn, hungry, thirsty, and loath to rise. A bluejay mocks him as a sleepy-head and warns that the early bear may catch the feast. Three tales make up the book, adding Cho-gay, an Indian boy ruler, and Kaw, the wise old crow. A drought year and a grizzly named Grayhead raise the stakes in the last tale. Young readers get warm woodland adventure with talking beasts.
61389-die-shadow:
Algis Budrys's story, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in May 1963, opens with a ship falling to Venus. David Greaves built the Defiance with his own fortune when no government would risk a manned rocket, and her engines have blown her apart. Battered in his seat, he drags himself from handhold to handhold toward the crash capsule.

Greaves pulls himself through the hatch and trips the lever that floods the capsule with Doctor Eckstrom's special anesthetic gas. The gas may, just barely, keep him alive through the smash. The magazine's blurb promises the rest of his arc: he began as a hero, and eons later, a universe away, he became instead a god.
61482-the-mystery-of-mrs-blencarrow:
The Mystery of Mrs Blencarrow is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, issued at Chicago by Donohue, Henneberry. The first chapter is called The Blencarrow Household. The house of Blencarrow stood in a pretty little park of its own. A bright little mountain river runs beside that park.

The house was as comfortable and handsome as a country gentleman could desire. Its county is left vague, between Cumberland, Westmoreland, and north Lancashire. The principal rooms stood on the slope of a hill, as north country houses do. Oliphant was a master of the domestic mystery in her long career. A widow’s secret and a household’s peace drive tales of this kind. The mystery here grows in drawing rooms, not in dark alleys.
61669-the-valley-of-the-shadow:
McNeile spins a tense house tale in The Valley of the Shadow, printed in New York with copyright in 1924. The tale opens at a dinner table in a big house off the Portsmouth road. Hilda Garling asks herself one thing for the twentieth time.

Why has her husband asked Jack Denver to stay? For a year the man has grown a recluse, shut in his room for days. He takes meals alone, and the house feels like a prison to his wife. Guests have failed, and trips to friends have failed too. Now chest pain, which he calls mere sour stomach, has forced a new step.
62288-billy-to-morrow:
Billy To-Morrow is a boys' novel by Sarah Pratt Carr, author of The Iron Way. McClurg published it at Chicago in 1909, with pictures by Relyea. The book is dedicated to one boy, strong, buoyant, and true. Its first chapter introduces the little earthquake girl. The Saturday Gang follows.

Chapters carry Billy through a fight, stormy seas, and a circus. A hidden hut, a haunted house, and a stand against fire fill the middle of the tale. A cat named Sir Thomas Katzenstein joins the crew. The bridge to safety closes the adventures. Carr writes wholesome western tales for boys, with the sea and the ranch both in reach.
63208-the-bee-master-of-warrilow:
Tickner Edwardes wrote The Bee-Master of Warrilow, a set of bee essays first printed in 1907 and enlarged in a third form in 1921. Edwardes was a fellow of the Entomological Society and author of a lore book on the honey bee. The essays first ran in the Pall Mall Gazette.

Thirty chapters move through the bee year, from February among the hives to the long winter night in the hive. Topics include the queen bee, honey flow, swarms, pollen, and old and new honey craft. Portraits of bee men of past days add charm to the practical lore. Bee keepers and nature lovers get both sound practice and fond lore in a warm country voice.
64251-this-finer-shadow:
Harlan Cozad McIntosh wrote a novel that John Cowper Powys praised in strong terms. The book came out in New York in 1941 with the Dial Press. Powys says he was proud to be among its first fans. He calls a man in the book, Roberts, a work of art. The book is given to Jane in its front pages.

Powys calls the tale strange, bold, and hard to shake off. He speaks of deep runs in the mind where dark wants hide. The hero's odd bent holds the reader, he says. Jane McIntosh holds the rights to the book. Readers who like dark mind tales get a rare, keen work.
64710-hostage-of-tomorrow:
Robert Abernathy wrote this science fiction story, printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1949. Its headnote asks whether Earth was on the wrong time-track, and whether Ray Manning could return a hundred years to find the answer.

The story opens in March 1945, with the wreck of the Third Reich across Europe. Manning, an MIT man kept a combat soldier by blarney, rides with a small column into the Black Forest. The mission is put plainly: while the army hands out body blows, they are after brains, hunting a Nazi-financed scientist with a hideout in the woods. The lieutenant orders captures, not kills. Readers get a time story rooted in the war's last weeks.
64803-in-the-earth-s-shadow:
In the Earth's Shadow is John Chapman's science fiction story, printed in Comet in December 1940. Its hero, Ferris, has sat alone for six years at Fuel Station 12. The station floats between Earth and Moon, serving the traffic of space. Ferris keeps the company afloat and thinks no one else can run the post.

Then the screen lights with Galsworth, the company head. A replacement will arrive within ten hours: Brooks, a green kid fresh from school. Ferris rages and packs, sure the boy will fail at the lonely work. The airlock hisses early, but the tall stranger who steps in is not Brooks. He wants fuel, and his tunic is ripped at the collar.
64955-the-fantasy-fan-volume-2-number-6-:
The Fantasy Fan for February 1935 is the last issue of a fan magazine for lovers of weird fiction, volume two, number six. It was edited by Charles Hornig, managing editor of Wonder Stories, and published from Elizabeth, New Jersey, at ten cents a copy. This number was billed as a short story number.

The editorial, headed Finale, breaks the news. This issue is the last. The magazine's life has run a year and a half, since September 1933. Its lesson, Hornig writes, is that there are not enough lovers of weird fiction willing to pay for a fan magazine. They had done all they could to keep it afloat. The printer, a fan himself, had charged far below his usual rates, but better work had taken his time. The Fantasy Fan is a founding document of science fiction fandom, and its farewell shows fan economics plainly.
65053-meet-me-in-tomorrow:
Guy Archette wrote the science fiction story Meet Me in Tomorrow, first printed in the magazine Imagination in December 1950. Andy Pearce, the young man at its center, is in love with Ellen Thorpe but can never tell her. The opening blurb gives the reason: she belongs to a world he is about to leave, and he knows his time with her is nearly done.

The story opens on a gravel road through green summer fields, with Pearce, Ellen, and Dave Fuller driving toward a picnic spot from Pearce's boyhood. Pearce is excited and more than a little afraid, and he promises the day will beat anything his friends can imagine. Talk in the car stays light, but his thoughts keep circling back to the secret he is carrying. Readers are set up for a parting that Pearce has planned and his friends cannot yet guess.
65129-how-to-study-fiorillo-a-detailed-d:
Edith Winn wrote this detailed analysis of how to practice the Fiorillo violin studies, based on the best teachings of modern violin playing. Carl Fischer published it at New York in 1913, dedicated to Davol Sanders. A life of Federigo Fiorillo opens the book.

Fiorillo was born in 1753 at Brunswick, son of a Neapolitan opera conductor, began on the mandolin, and turned to the violin. He conducted at Riga from 1783, played with success in Paris in 1785, and appeared in London in Salomon's quartet, his last public performance a viola concerto in 1794. Winn calls his Thirty-six Caprices the one work known and valued by every violin player, ranking with the classical studies of Kreutzer and Rode. She then takes the studies one by one, beginning with the first etude's Largo, played forte and very slowly for a full, even tone.
65229-hold-back-tomorrow:
Kris Neville wrote this science fiction story for Imagination in September 1951. Margy knows it is good to be young, the blurb says, and she never wants to grow old. In her world, growing old and dying takes five centuries, and that must not happen to her.

Clyde greets Margy bashfully beside a low, white stone wall around the schoolyard. A carefully kept forest and lakes lie beyond the wall in the scene. She answers him politely, feels a small flutter of unnamed fear, and tells him he may sit there, since she does not own the wall. Youth, time and fear meet quietly.
66394-the-dangerous-scarecrow:
Carl Jacobi's Dangerous Scarecrow ran in Imagination in August 1954. Two scarecrows stand on adjacent farms across a road: Maudsley in the cornfield, his hand nailed to a pie tin that catches the moonlight, and Trask, wearing a strip of bright foil. Jimmy Tapping and his sister Stella treat both strawmen as playmates and dress them with gifts. The headnote warns that Jimmy gave a knife to one of them. On an October evening the family drives home between the shocked fields.

Jimmy stays awake that night, listening to the old house creak in the wind. He takes the silver spyglass his father gave him at Christmas and studies the two figures in the moonlight. Something about Maudsley makes him wipe the lens and focus again with a puzzled frown. Jacobi builds the tale's dread out of a boy's night watching.
66815-in-caverns-below:
Stanton Coblentz wrote In Caverns Below, a science novel run in Wonder Stories in the spring of nineteen thirty-five and later issued as Hidden World. Frank Comstock tells the tale. He and Philip Clay, mining engineers and close friends, were given up as lost five years before. In the autumn of nineteen twenty-nine they vanished in a silver mine in Nevada.

The world thought a cave-in had crushed them past all finding, since no trace of their bodies was found. Comstock says they lived most of those five years in a far land of wonders and fear. They found things, he claims, not matched since Columbus sailed west. Now back as if from the grave, he sets down how they fell into that world and what they met there.
67196-observations-on-the-terataspis-gra:
Observations on the Terataspis Grandis treats the largest known trilobite, written by Clarke, a New York geologist. The paper was sent to the state geologist in December 1890. Clarke opens by noting that most giant trilobites rest on mere scraps of shell. Restoring their true size, he warns, takes strong mental effort.

He then surveys the giants of past reports across the old faunas. One kind from the Braintree beds may have reached eighteen inches long. A near whole specimen from the Saint John beds measured fifteen inches. Locke's great Ohio form and its huge tail shield get full treatment. Clarke's own subject crowns the list as the largest of all. The paper serves students of the oldest seas and their strange armoured life.
67266-dogs-always-know:
Dogs Always Know is a love story by Elisabeth Sanxay Holding. Its heading promises that huge Captain MacGregor barges into a dignified romance with a cargo of humour, matched against little Leroy's dramatic dog. The tale opens with two people who do not like each other. Miss Selby comes from Boston, and Mr. Anderson comes from New York.

Miss Selby, just then, likes no one who is not from Boston. She measures everyone against her mother, grandmother, and two aunts at home. Anderson dislikes her chiefly because she plainly dislikes him. The story sets this stiff pair on a course where pride must soften, with the captain and the dog doing much of the work.
67514-the-house-of-the-arrow:
Mason published 'The House of the Arrow' with the George Doran Company of New York in 1924, a Hanaud case. Chapter One, 'Letters of Mark,' opens at Frobisher and Haslitt, solicitors on the east side of Russell Square. The firm prides itself on its French connection, dating from 1806, when James Frobisher organized the escape of hundreds of detained British subjects.

Jeremy Haslitt looks after that side himself, and on an April morning only one French letter lies in his batch. It is addressed in a spidery, uncontrolled hand with a Dijon postmark, written from La Maison Grenelle, his client the widow Harlowe's house, but not by her. The signature reads Boris Waberski. Contents ahead promise Betty Harlowe, a clock upon a cabinet, the breaking of seals, and the finding of the arrow.
67835-better-days-or-a-millionaire-of-to:
Better Days, or A Millionaire of To-morrow, is a reform novel by Thomas Fitch and Anna Fitch. The Better Days Publishing Company issued it at San Francisco in 1891. A verse motto says philosophy's province is the conduct of social life. The book is dedicated to the eight thousand millionaires of America. If one of them disposes of part of his fortune well, the dedication hopes. Wage workers would then be helped to help themselves. The pages will not have been written in vain, it says.

The first chapter opens with the earth trembling under men's feet. Professor John Thornton calls Chicago the typical American city. New York and San Francisco may be classed as metropolitan, he says. Philadelphia, Saint Louis, and New Orleans are local, he judges. The novel argues its reform through story and debate. It belongs to the era's flood of economic fiction.
68203-don-t-look-now:
Don't Look Now is a science fiction tale by Henry Kuttner, first printed in Startling Stories in March 1948. The blurb warns that the man beside you may be a Martian. It opens in a bar, where a man in a brown suit studies his face in the mirror. Beside him, a drinker named Lyman has talked for a quarter of an hour. At last Lyman speaks the title words. One of them was sitting right there, he says, and has just gone out.

The man in brown proves to be a reporter. Lyman claims that Martians own the world in secret. A few men know it, he says, and Wells was one of them. With Orson it was just a gag, but Wells knew or guessed the truth. Lyman wants proof brought out before it can be stopped.
68451-mirrors-of-moscow:
Louise Bryant wrote Mirrors of Moscow, portraits of the men who ruled new Russia. Thomas Seltzer issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty three. Cesare drew its five plates of the chiefs she met. Bryant had watched the revolution at close range in Petrograd.

Lenin and his aides fill the first long portrait in the book. Dzerzhinsky and the dread Extraordinary Commission come next in line. Lunacharsky speaks for schools, art, and the new culture there. Kalinin stands for the peasants, Kollontai for free women of Russia. Trotsky, war lord of the Reds, gets his own full chapter. Enver Pasha, Tikhon of the Church, and Chicherin follow in turn. Lenin rides a runaway horse, Bryant says, as Russia bucks below. One unlit flame in him burns for the next age of man, she writes.
68565-to-the-sons-of-tomorrow:
To the Sons of Tomorrow is a tale by Irving Cox from Rocket Stories magazine. Beecham drew the pictures for the July 1953 printing of the tale. The starship Olympus can never return to her home planet again. Her crew must live out their lives among this new world's savages. Captain Theusaman hopes to wean them from superstition toward knowledge in time.

Baiel protests when Theusaman orders an emergency landing on that world. The ship lies ninety-three million light years from Earth by his count. Dorsal tubes are blown and the emergency fuel is lost for good. Without fresh fissionable stuff, no hope of return home remains at all. The planet shows air like Earth's and rich fissionable rock below. But if their machines cannot win it, landing strands them for life. The Space Code and its forms hold the crew's manners in space.
69118-the-west-from-a-car-window:
Richard Harding Davis rode the trains of the West and wrote what he saw for Harper, in a book copyrighted in 1892. Texas, he jokes, is given on the back of a railroad map as a hundred thousand square miles larger than all the eastern and middle states put together.

The pieces run from San Antonio to Corpus Christi. Davis writes of troops on the border and of a civilian at an army post. He visits a new mining camp and a city only three years old. Ranch life in Texas and a stay on an Indian reservation follow. Pictures fill the pages, of bucking bronchos, rangers in camp, mines, and army parades.
69185-tales-of-the-long-bow:
Tales of the Long Bow is a set of tall tales by the English writer Chesterton. A New York house brought the book out in nineteen twenty five. Each tale turns on a deed held past do or past belief, the front words say. Eight parts bear names of stiff men of the League of the Long Bow. Colonel Crane leads off with a show that will not pass muster.

That first tale starts on a prim road at church hour on a Sunday morn. Crane, a staid past chief of war, walks to church as his flock of kin do. No mark sets him off from his mates save that he shows less. Green, Hood, Pierce, and White fill the next parts of the set. A last part gives the league its own final stiff word.
69277-sunshine-and-snow:
Harold Bindloss wrote boys adventure before he wrote the northern novels that made his name, and Sunshine and Snow shows both trades at once. The frontispiece catches men found hiding down the fore-hold, and eight illustrations carry a story that runs from an English school to a cattle ship and a blizzard.

Charley Gordon of Firdene School has just taken the prizes and read his essay to the school. The chapters ahead put him through a paper-chase, a collision at sea, stolen cattle, adverse fortune, and the snows coming down. Bindloss writes the schoolboy code of honor straight into the storm, and the weather does the moral testing.
693-the-autobiography-of-a-quack-and-the:
S. Weir Mitchell, a noted American doctor, paired two tales that first ran unsigned in the Atlantic Monthly. The first is the boastful memoir of a quack, a fake healer who lives by tricks, fine talk, and the trust of the sick. The second is the case notes of George Dedlow, a soldier who wakes after battle to find his limbs gone.

Mitchell recast the quack tale at length and notes that the Dedlow case was taken by many readers as real, with money raised for the sufferer. The pair shows both sides of his art: satire on medical fraud, and a sober study of pain and loss after war. Together they mark an early step in American medical fiction.
69649-the-ranch-girls-and-the-silver-arr:
The Ranch Girls and the Silver Arrow, by Margaret Vandercook, was printed by the John C Winston Company at Philadelphia, with a copyright of 1921 and art by Edwin J Prittie. Four girls lead their ponies down a tight canyon, cliffs high on each side, a stream at their feet. They are lost, and Lina owns it while Jeanette will not. To be late this day is the rub: their father comes home with a new wife.

Jim Colter of the Rainbow Ranch has wed Jacqueline Ralston Kent, once a Ranch Girl herself, far his junior. His girls run fifteen, fourteen, twelve, and eight. The plates show the find that names the book: an odd arrow, a treasure. A young Indian searches the rocks in one. Girls of the age got canyon, kin, and a strange prize.
70164-the-best-vegetarian-dishes-i-know:
The Best Vegetarian Dishes I Know, by Jeanne Jardine, was printed in London by J M Dent and Sons in 1910. A kitchen verse heads the book, that the business of the kitchen is great, and it is fit that men should eat. The recipes run from artichokes to eggs and beyond, all without meat.

The contents open with artichoke curry, artichoke and egg fricassee, and artichoke fritters. Artichokes au gratin, artichokes a la Mornay, and an artichoke and potato pie follow. Baked beans with spinach and eggs, baked eggs with spaghetti, and batter balls fill the next lines. Broad beans in Italian style, butter beans moulded, and cabbage stuffed with nuts stand in the mid list. Carrots in a rice border, cassolettes with peas, and cauliflower in batter come in turn. Cooks get a full meatless kitchen of 1910.
70580-no-war-tomorrow:
Wallace West's No War Tomorrow, billed as a feature novel of days to come, ran in Science Fiction Quarterly in May 1951. Captain Frank Sage of the Space Patrol pushes through the double safety doors of the Moon Station Cafe and orders black coffee, ham and eggs, and apple pie from Old Tom.

Sage is pushing off as soon as his ship is refueled, troubled by the Big Shots on Venus. United Stars will not use the Patrol to clean them out, and Sadie, Tom's daughter, agrees with United Stars. Tom answers that Wildoatia is the safety valve of United Stars, where incorrigibles who hate a peaceful, well-ordered civilization go to sow their wild oats.
70971-the-east-i-know:
Paul Claudel wrote prose pieces on the East, rendered by Teresa Frances and William Rose Benét and printed at Yale in 1914. The pieces date from 1895 to 1900. Short works bear titles such as The Cocoa Palm, The Pagoda, and The City at Night. Gardens, the feast of the dead, and thoughts on the sea follow.

Later pieces treat theaters, tombs, the banyan, and the great sea. Months of the year, painting, rain, and night on the verandah all appear. Claudel writes in brief, dense images rather than straight travel report. A note says he worked for twenty years in near obscurity before fame came.
71381-daisy-of-old-meadow:
Agnes Giberne writes a village tale in Daisy of Old Meadow, published at London by James Nisbet and Company. Scripture mottoes from Job and Matthew, both against laying up treasure on earth, announce the theme, and a frontispiece shows Daisy Meads and John Davis lying senseless on the half-made hay. Chapters follow Daisy's needs and troubles, Old Isaac, and a rice pudding.

Betsy Simmons opens the story with a character of the miser: the crookedest, crabbedest, cantankerousest old fellow she ever met, who pokes into everything before spending a penn'orth. Against him stands Miss Meads, a little angel in Betsy's telling.
72428-pyramids-of-snow:
Pyramids of Snow, a novel by Edith Metcalfe, was published in London, New York, and Melbourne in 1903. A title motto from William de Britaine warns the gambler: vice will swallow him like a quicksand, or his gains will melt faster than they came, like pyramids of snow. A front plate quotes a threat to have a guest put out.

Twenty-seven chapters open at the Casino at Monte Carlo, where an incident passes most guests by. Heads promise fraud, bigamy, murder, a found body, flight, an arrest, and a trial. A faithful servant, an unexpected will, and a place of peace close the tale. Metcalfe mixes casino glitter with crime and fate in a brisk Edwardian romance.
72600-the-trumpeter-of-krakow:
The Trumpeter of Krakow is a tale of the fifteenth century by Eric Kelly. A Polish artist in Krakow drew the prints for the book. Rights date the work to the year nineteen twenty eight. A later print run of the work bears the year nineteen fifty seven.

A young trumpeter in a high tower gives the tale its heart and name. Parts treat a man who would not sell his squash, an herb man, and a saint. Street fights, a loft of dark arts, and a foe with a scarred face follow. An old tower call broke off in mid note in a past raid on the town. Honour, craft, and the old town ways shape the prized boys tale.
72697-the-vow:
Paul Trent's Vow came from Grosset and Dunlap in New York in a fifth edition. John Rae supplied a color frontispiece. Words lettered under that picture give the novel its title: give her back to me, and I vow the rest of my days to your service. The copy carries a 1911 copyright from the Stokes company. Trent dedicates the novel to Ethel.

The story opens on a dull November day. John Gaunt, a self-made millionaire, sits flushed by firelight. He confesses that money has bought him acquaintances but never a friend. He believes he has found a confidant in Lady Mildred Blythe. Braithwaite then comes begging again. Gaunt repays an old service once more and signs a check for a hundred pounds. He tells Braithwaite plainly that it is the last penny he will ever get.
73005-pussy-meow:
Pussy Meow: The Autobiography of a Cat, by Patteson, was published at Philadelphia in 1901, with an opening essay by Sarah Bolton. A preface tells how the book began. In the fall of 1895, a group at a convention in Cleveland discussed Black Beauty and Beautiful Joe.

One hoped that, as the horse and the dog had now secured a public hearing, someone would undertake the same for the cat. That same evening Pussy Meow began writing her story. Its only object, the preface says, is to breathe out the joys, sorrows, and longings of a misunderstood fellow creature. It seeks for cats the consideration humanity owes to the dumb. Contents run from early recollections through farm experiences, companions, Christmas, great sorrow, and a joyful reunion, to a new home. Readers get a cat life in the Black Beauty manner.
73256-told-in-the-gardens-of-araby-untra:
Told in the Gardens of Araby is a set of eastern tales by Izora Chandler and Mary Montgomery. Its title claims the tales were untranslated until now. The New York issue is from Eaton and Mains. A prelude paints the garden where the tales are told.

That garden lies within white walls topped with red tiles. Palms, cypress, fig, quince, orange, and pomegranate shade it. Roses and cabbages, lilies and onions grow side by side. The tales that follow bear the stamp of the place. They include the Emerald Roc, a girl who had her wish, and a girl who did not. One tale joins a crying pomegranate with a laughing bear. The set ends with a crystal kiosk and a diamond ship.
73711-tracks-in-the-snow:
Tracks in the Snow is a tale of a crime, shaped from the hand writ of a priest by Benson. It came out at London, New York, and Bombay in the first years of the last age. Its gift word is in Latin, made out to a lady.

Its first page sets the crime in plain terms. On the morn of a day in the depth of the cold months, a man was found slain in his bed. His house stood in a parish where the priest who tells the tale then held his post. Much dark hung on the facts of his death. It was to the priests hands, he says, that chance threw the clue. The death of his own friend, on the eve of a full bloom of his gifts, lies too close for full due in his words.
73851-brazil-today-and-tomorrow:
Elliott wrote Brazil Today and Tomorrow, first published in 1917 and revised in 1922. Elliott was literary editor of the Pan American Magazine and had written Chile, Today and Tomorrow. Photographs show Botafogo Bay and the peaks above Rio de Janeiro.

An introduction surveys Brazil's great extent, its virgin interior, and its mix of soils, climates, and industries. Chapter heads in the contents trace the land from Cabral's landing through the Dutch wars and Dom Pedro the Second. Later chapters treat settlement by Swiss, Germans, Italians, and Japanese. Social life, saints' days, and the place of women also come under review.
73875-the-ceramic-art-of-great-britain-f:
The Ceramic Art of Great Britain, by Llewellynn Jewitt, was published in London in 1878, in two volumes. Jewitt traces pottery and porcelain works from pre-historic times down to his own day. The first volume is one part of a large work with near two thousand pictures cut in the text.

The title page promises a history of the old and new works of the kingdom, and of their goods of every class. Jewitt held posts in learned groups for the study of old things, in Britain and abroad. He gave the book to a head of the Minton firm, in praise of work done for the art. Readers get a vast Victorian guide to British pots, makers, and wares.
74068-the-ceramic-art-of-great-britain-f:
The Ceramic Art of Great Britain is a full past of pot and china work by Llewellynn Jewitt. It runs from old times down to the age of the book itself. This text is the second of its two books, printed at London in eighteen seventy eight. Near two thousand cuts fill its pages with works of each class. Jewitt held posts in old lore groups of England and of far lands.

Book two walks shire by shire through the pot works of the realm. Tyne, Tees, and Wear works open the tour in the north east. Liverpool delft ware and print ware fill the next long part. Derby china and its merged Chelsea works get a full part as well. Each works gets its own tale of firms, hands, and wares.
74531-chile-today-and-tomorrow:
Chile Today and Tomorrow is a land book by Elliott, out from Macmillan in nineteen twenty two. Elliott wrote a like book on Brazil in the same mold in past years. Part one paints the land in north, mid, and south bands of hue. Clime, wet and dry year turns, and far flung towns fill that part. Past part runs from Inca rule through the Spain years to free rule.

Sea guest part treats Drake, Cavendish, and the loss of the Wager ship. Church court years in Chile get a part of their own in scheme. Magellan strait first sails and Port Famine fill a mid part. Tacna claim strife with Peru fills a grave part on bounds and salt earth. Mine part treats salt cake, copper, iron, and coal in rank.
74769-the-woman-of-to-morrow:
The Woman of To Morrow is a book of essays for women by Helen M Winslow, published in New York in nineteen hundred five. Winslow dedicates it to her sisters, and a first impression date of September that year is printed. Chapters open with the woman of to morrow herself, then turn to individual responsibility. Our relation to life, friends, and enemies follow in order.

Mrs Gummidge, a figure of self pity from Dickens, gets a chapter as a warning type. Mental attitudes, the essentials of happiness, worry, and solitude are all treated. Women's clubs, the ethics of clothes, public duties, and housekeeping close the visible list. Cheerful self rule for a new century is Winslow's gospel.
75097-flying-down-a-rainbow:
Flying Down a Rainbow, by Homer King Gordon, author of The Sky Pirate, is an aviation adventure from the early days of commercial flying. Its hero, Jimmy Devlin, pays four hundred dollars for a wrecked biplane in Hangar Number Three at Pacific Field, and the other pilots laugh. Jimmy laughs too, but hopefully.

Two months of work, yards of fabric, and buckets of dope make the wreck fly, and a government man licenses it for passengers. Then business fails: rival pilots with new planes mock his Calico Peacock, and fares stay away. Gordon frames the tale with an old timer's saying that gold flirts for years, then throws herself on a stranger.
76352-the-world-below:
The World Below is a scientific romance by Fowler Wright, published at London in 1929. Books for Today issued it; this copy is the second impression. Wright had written Deluge and The Island of Captain Sparrow. A long list of his fiction, verse, and translations fronts the book. The contents name only Book One, The Amphibians.

Twenty five chapters of that book are listed before the text. An empty dawn, an opal way, and an invisible bridge begin the descent. Frog mouths, a tunnel of fear, and capture follow. The killers and their arsenal dominate the middle chapters. One chapter pauses on the ethics of violence. A duel in the night and an escape close the listed run. Wright imagines a far future earth ruled by strange amphibian powers. Human travellers must fight their way through it.
76634-lillian-s-vow:
Mrs Burke Collins wrote Lillian's Vow, a romance in the Sweetheart Series priced at twenty-five cents, printed at New York in 1898 by George Munro's Sons. The series lists popular tales by Charles Garvice, Laura Jean Libbey, and Charlotte Braeme in photogravure covers. Lillian's Vow stands among dozens of love stories sold by subscription.

Sweetheart novels promised handsome print, large clear type, and good paper at low cost for wide reading. Vows, hearts' desires, ransoms, coronets of shame, and struggles for a heart fill the catalogue around this title. Collins's tale follows the series pattern of love tested by class, secrecy, and rival claims on the heroine. Dime romance readers get period sentimental fiction.
77340-bacchus-or-wine-to-day-and-to-morr:
Morton Shand, author of A Book of Wine and A Book of French Wines, wrote this essay on wine today and tomorrow. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Company published it at London, and Dutton at New York. A line from Hafiz heads it: put a cup of wine into my hand that I may cast off the cloak of hypocrisy.

Shand opens by attacking American Prohibition. He calls the Volstead Act a hysterical piece of amateur legislation, hung like a tavern sign over all wines good and bad. The war that was to end war was also to end wine, he writes, and American crusaders meant to make the world as safe for teetotalism as for democracy. The Latin nations refused conversion and kept their vineyards, and Shand argues that the advertisement Prohibition gave wine has assured its future until the next Puritan revival.
77657-afterglow:
Julia Dorr wrote Afterglow, a book of later poems published by Scribner in New York in 1900. A dedication verse promises the spoils of later years, half sunshine and half tears. The contents list some fifty poems. Inconsistency opens the volume, and titles such as The Sanctuary Lamp, Three Crosses, and The Sacramental Hymn show the devotional cast of much of the book. Other poems treat Bar Harbor, Spain, and the death of Spenser.

The first poem begins with a day fairer than other days, when mountain passes glow and dim valleys wake at morning's first rays. Dorr wrote in the received forms of her century: sonnets, hymns, and meditative lyrics in measured stanzas. She was among the best-known American women poets of the late nineteenth century. Afterglow gathers the verse of her old age, quiet and faithful in tone.
7774-the-journal-of-arthur-stirling-the-:
Upton Sinclair edits and condenses The Journal of Arthur Stirling, subtitled The Valley of the Shadow, with an introductory sketch. Stirling, known to barely a dozen people in a huge city, was Sinclair's close friend, a self-taught man who worked many hard jobs by day and studied by night.

He taught himself five languages, knew more great poetry by heart than any man of letters Sinclair knew, and wrote a blank-verse tragedy called The Captive. The journal records a life of fierce artistic devotion, poverty, and hope, and stands as a portrait of talent unnoticed by the world.
77895-the-hermit-of-turkey-hollow:
Hermit of Turkey Hollow is a legal tale by Arthur Train, published by Scribner in 1921. Its subtitle calls it the story of an alibi, an exploit of Ephraim Tutt. Tutt, attorney and counselor at law, is Train recurring hero of courtroom fiction. A song about a grandfather clock that stopped when the old man died heads the tale.

Chapter one opens by defining alibi in law as a plea of being elsewhere. That plea, and the fact behind it, form the hinge of the whole case. Tutt must test a hermit story against time, place, and stubborn small town fact. Train mixes humour with shrewd law in this short Tutt adventure.
77966-spooky-hollow:
Carolyn Wells published Spooky Hollow with Lippincott in 1923, a Fleming Stone story. The series list at the front advertises the baffling detective stories in which Stone, the great American detective, displays his remarkable ingenuity. Feathers Left Around, Raspberry Jam, and The Diamond Pin keep it company.

The contents begin with Prout, who has a fare. The guest at Greatlarch, Rosemary, and a mysterious death follow. Where was Johnson, the fifth chapter asks. Wells wrote Stone as the thinking machine of American detection, summoned when the local mind gives out. Spooky Hollow is a country-house title, and the hollow obliges with atmosphere. Her mysteries run on logic and timetable, and this one, dedicated to her friend Julie Staniford, follows the formula with a ghost story's trimmings.
78406-the-poetical-works-of-henry-wadswo:
Poems of Henry Longfellow fill this large book, reprinted in London in 1889. The text was checked against his last revised American form. The front note says early and late poems both stand here. Some poems had not run in other such books before.

Early poems and Voices of the Night open the volume in order. Ballads bring tales like The Wreck of the Hesperus to the fore. Poems on slavery voice grief for slaves in swamp and field. Long loved songs of home, faith, and loss fill the rest. Frederick Warne issued this London printing in the Imperial Poets line.
79340-d-p-from-tomorrow:
D P From Tomorrow, a tale by Mack Reynolds, opens in a newspaper city room. The little man of the head note was very sincere, as so many of them are. A phone rings and Ed Kerry picks it up and says Daily Star. A caller wants to know when Lord Byron died, to settle a bet.

Sam at the rewrite desk answers at once that he died on April 19th, 1824. Jake the city editor asks Sam how he knows such a fact. Sam shrugs that he just happened to know it when asked. Jake muses that no information makes less difference than when Byron died. A displaced person from tomorrow hides behind that glib memory, the tale hints.
7953-behind-the-bungalow:
Writing as Eha, Edward Hamilton Aitken gathered these papers from the Times of India into a book first published for readers of the Bombay Presidency. Illustrated by F. C. Macrae and here in its sixth edition of 1897, it describes life behind an Anglo-Indian bungalow. The servants, or nowkers, run the household, from the bearer who brings tea and slippers to the many hands behind every daily task. The Indian servant, Aitken notes, shows much the same traits wherever he is found.

The sketches are humorous and affectionate, though written from the employer's side of the veranda. They preserve a vivid picture of colonial domestic life: its routines, misunderstandings, and small diplomacies. Modern readers will enjoy the wit while also seeing, clearly, the unequal world that made such households possible.
8084-hunting-with-the-bow-arrow:
Saxton Pope wrote this book on hunting with the bow and arrow, with forty-eight illustrations, dedicating it to Robin Hood, a spirit that dwells in the heart of every youth. Its chapters begin with the story of Ishi, the last Yana Indian, his bow and arrow, and his methods of hunting. Then turn to archery in general: how to make a bow and arrow, equipment, how to shoot, and the principles of hunting. Later chapters cover raccoon, deer, bear, mountain lions, grizzly, and Alaskan adventures.

Pope, a physician and friend of Ishi, helped revive traditional archery in America, and his book mixes anthropology with practical instruction. It teaches the craft from the ground up, with respect for the Native teacher at its centre. For archers and readers of outdoor literature, it remains a foundational and humane classic.
8413-the-bishop-s-shadow:
I. T. Thurston wrote The Bishop's Shadow for young readers, with illustrations by M. Eckerson. Contents open with a lost pocketbook, Nan's new home, an accident, and Tode meeting the bishop, and the epigraph speaks of shadows: our influence may fall where we can never be. The bishop's shadow, in other words, is the good a life casts beyond itself.

Thurston, author of Boys of the Central and A Genuine Lady, writes in the wholesome children's tradition of the day, with plucky young people and moral lessons worn lightly. Readers of old-fashioned juvenile fiction will find a gentle, earnest story, where small kindnesses and accidents shape lives. It is a period piece, best read as such.
849-the-idle-thoughts-of-an-idle-fellow:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote these essays by an idle fellow, who defends idleness as a fine art. He muses on being idle, on love, on cats and dogs, and on the vanity of busy folk, in prose that is witty, confessional, and warm. The dedication, to a friend of prosperous and evil days, sets the joking tone.

Jerome's idle fellow is no fool: he watches human nature with a sharp eye and a kind heart. The essays, short and urbane, made Jerome famous before Three Men in a Boat. The book charms readers who enjoy light philosophy, where a lazy afternoon yields more truth than a week of hustle.
8902-the-flight-of-the-shadow:
George MacDonald opens The Flight of the Shadow with Mrs Day beginning the story, followed by Miss Martha Moon, an uncle, his room, and the narrator's first secret. Losing herself, a mirror, Thanatos and Zoe, a garden, and once more a secret carry the early chapters, before the mole burrows, a letter arrives, and old love meets new. Mother and uncle, the time between, fault and no fault, a summons, and John seeing something raise the tension.

John taken ill, a strange visit, and a foiled attempt continue the mystery, as a shadow, literal and moral, pursues the family. MacDonald blends domestic realism with fairy-tale dread, in the manner of his Scottish romances. Readers who know MacDonald from children's books will find a darker, adult novel here, concerned with conscience, inheritance, and the secrets that shape a household across generations.
9080-the-children-s-own-longfellow:
This illustrated gift book gathers poems by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow chosen for young readers. It holds favorites that American children long learned by heart. The Wreck of the Hesperus leads the set. The Village Blacksmith and Paul Revere's Ride follow, with parts of Evangeline and The Song of Hiawatha.

The picks favor clear stories, strong rhythms, and scenes a child can picture, from a ship in a storm to a smith at his forge. Longfellow's fame as America's household poet rests in part on just such verse. The book still works as a first meeting with a poet whose lines once rang in schoolrooms across the land.
9155-heather-and-snow:
George MacDonald wrote this Scots novel of heather hills, snow, and strong-willed folk. Its people include David and his daughter, Kirsty, Francis Gordon, and Phemy Craig. A runaway race opens the tale, and love, pride, and kinship drive it on through storms, abductions, and a race with death.

MacDonald sets the story in a Scotland of crofts, kirks, and winter roads, with Scots speech flavoring the talk. Kirsty's grit and heart anchor the plot. Readers who love Victorian tales of character and place will find here a warm, rugged story.
9786-love-s-shadow:
Ada Leverson wrote Love's Shadow in 1908, the first book of her Little Ottleys series. Edith and Bruce Ottley, young and pretty, live in a very new, very small, very white flat in Knightsbridge. Bruce begs Edith not to make him late at the office, while Edith, cheerful and intelligent, hides a subtler mind. A Shakespeare verse on love like a shadow fronts the book.

The novel follows the Ottleys' marriage through letters, mornings, and social calls, with wit as its chief weapon. Leverson writes with light, ironic grace, fond of her foolish, charming folk. A reader gets a witty Edwardian comedy of marriage, and the start of a beloved comic series.
aaron-trow:
Anthony Trollope opens with a warning about Bermuda: he will never regard those islets as the Fortunate Islands of the ancients. Getting in or out, he writes, tries any sailor's patience, and Caliban fits the place better than Ariel. On one of those islands lives a quiet clerk, Caleb Morton, and his wife, in a lonely house.

Aaron Trow, an escaped convict from the hulks, breaks into that house by night, and the tale tightens into a hunt across the island's cedar groves and inlets. Trollope, best known for cathedral towns and drawing rooms, here writes a grim, compact story of terror and pursuit. It appeared in his Tales of All Countries of 1864.
and-even-now:
Max Beerbohm gathered essays written over ten years and dated each one, as his note from Rapallo in 1920 explains. The contents run from A Relic of 1918 to pieces on hosts and guests, servants, going out for a walk, and laughter. An old portmanteau found in a cupboard opens the first essay.

Beerbohm writes on books within books, a clergyman, speaking French, and a house among the pines, always with the same light, exact prose and gentle irony. The war years shadow several pieces without darkening their poise. The book shows the essayist in maturity, amused by the world and quietly sad at its changes.
at-the-foot-of-the-rainbow:
Gene Stratton-Porter set At the Foot of the Rainbow along Indiana's Wabash River, among trappers, fishermen, and the birds of the Limberlost country she made famous. The contents promise rat-catchers, coon hunts, kingfishers, and black bass, mixed with the Malone family's troubles. Dannie Micrander and Jimmy Malone, boyhood friends, stand at the center.

Jimmy drinks, neglects his wife Mary, and drifts toward ruin while Dannie quietly loves Mary and holds to his renunciation. Fishing and trapping scenes carry the nature writing Stratton-Porter readers expected, exact about seasons and animal habits. The closing chapters bring confession, sacrifice, and the pot of gold the title promises, in her warm moral style.
behind-the-bungalow:
Edward Hamilton Aitken, writing as EHA, collected these sketches of Indian domestic service from the Times of India, here in a sixth edition from Thacker in 1897. Aitken warns that they were written for the Bombay Presidency, but the Indian servant, the nowker, shows the same traits everywhere. F. C. Macrae illustrates the bungalow world of masters at ease and boys in attendance.

Engaging a Boy opens the set: the narrator stretched six feet over an easy chair, tea ministered by Canjee, slippers placed, in absolute repose. Promotion poisons contentment in the middle sketch: a servant raised to eight rupees burns for ten, then sees the strange, beautiful hope of becoming a Naik dawning. Aitken writes colonial household comedy with a naturalist's eye — affectionate, exact, and of its empire's moment.
blacky-the-crow:
Thornton W. Burgess opens Blacky the Crow with a warning about his hero's eyes. Blacky is forever spying out things never meant for his sharp eyes. In this he resembles his cousin Sammy Jay, Burgess writes. Winter locks up the Big River and the Smiling Pool, and food is scarce.

Blacky flies to a lonesome corner of the Green Forest where Redtail the Hawk once nested. In the old nest he finds eggs that are not Redtail's, and a mystery of the duck family begins. Ducky the Gadwall and his mate have trusted the empty nest. Blacky's discovery sets hunters, crows, and conscience at odds. Burgess tells the tale for young children, in short chapters with a naturalist's accuracy. Peter Rabbit and Happy Jack Squirrel comment from the sidelines, as his readers expected.
britannica-1911-bredow:
Bredow is a German village in Prussia that sits just north of Stettin and serves as a suburb of that port city. Its fame rests on heavy industry rather than size or age. The Vulcan iron-works and shipbuilding yards there built some of the largest liners in the German merchant fleet of the day.

Three named ships anchor the account: the Deutschland of 1900, the Kaiserin Augusta Victoria of 1906 and the George Washington of 1908. The last, at 722 feet long and 27,000 tons, ranked as the largest vessel in the German mercantile marine. Sugar works, cement works and other factories round out a short entry centred on shipbuilding.
britannica-1911-chang-chow:
Chang-chow is a town of China, in the province of Fu-kien. It stands on a branch of the Lung Kiang, 35 miles west of Amoy. A wall of four and a half miles runs round it, though much open ground lies inside. The streets are paved with granite but are very dirty. A strange bridge of wood planks crosses the river. The planks rest on twenty-five piles of stones, set about 30 feet apart, and the bridge runs 800 feet in all.

Chang-chow is a centre of the silk trade and does a wide trade in many lines. Brick works and sugar works are among its chief plants. Its people are put at about a million. The article is short and gives the town's place, wall, bridge, trade, and works as its main facts, with no more on its past or its rule.
britannica-1911-chepstow:
Chepstow is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town and river port in Monmouthshire, England. It stands on the Wye, two miles above the river's junction with the Severn. Its urban district counted 3067 people in 1901. The town occupies the slope of a hill on the left bank, amid beautiful scenery. The church of St Mary began as the chapel of a Benedictine priory of Norman foundation.

The castle is still a magnificent pile. William Fitz Osbern founded it in the eleventh century, and it was almost wholly rebuilt in the thirteenth. It covers about three acres on a cliff top above the Wye. An iron bridge of 1816 and a tubular railway bridge by Brunel cross the river. The tide in the deep, narrow channel rises suddenly and high, forming a dangerous bore. Exports are timber, bark, iron, coal, and cider. Some shipbuilding is carried on.
britannica-1911-curassow:
Curassows are a group of large game birds of South America, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes their form and habits. Among the largest and finest of the region's game birds, they stand in the place the pheasants hold in the Old World. Many rival the turkey in size, with short wings and a long, broad tail.

The entry notes that, save for one species, they live only in the tropical forests east of the Andes, down to Paraguay. They move in small flocks, live in trees, and roost and nest in the branches. Their neat nests are woven of thin branches and grass stems, lined with leaves. They feed on fruits, seeds, and insects, and are often tamed.
britannica-1911-fallow:
Fallow ground gets a clear farming entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Fallow means land that is ploughed and tilled but left unsown, often for a year. The rest lets the soil break up, take in air, and lose its weeds. The entry also traces the word to an old English root tied to ploughing.

Farmers have rested soil since ancient times, the entry notes. It points to the rest year set for land under Mosaic law. New crop plans and manures later cut the need for bare fallow. Bare fallow wastes a season and lets plant food wash away. Green fallow and bastard fallow get short accounts too.
britannica-1911-fellow:
Fellow is a 1911 Britannica entry on the sense and past use of one common English word. It starts with the plain sense of a partner, mate, or friend. The Old English root meant a man who put money or goods into a shared plan. From that root came its use for a member of a college.

The entry then sets out how Oxford, Cambridge, and Trinity College in Dublin used the term. A fellow was a senior member, picked by the college, who shared in its rule. He also drew a fixed sum from college funds. Some fellows taught as tutors, and learned groups took up the word too.
britannica-1911-fuchow:
Fuchow, also Foochow, is a city of China, capital of Fu-kien province and a chief port open to foreign trade. It stands on the river Min about 35 miles from the sea, 140 miles north of Amoy. The walled city proper lies some three miles from the north bank, its wall 30 feet high making a circuit of over five miles with seven gateways.

Suburbs fill the ground to the river, the island of Nantai, and the south bank, and a long stone bridge joins the shores. The great arsenal at Pagoda Island, founded in 1867 under French engineers, built small gunboats before French ships partly destroyed it in 1884. The port opened to European commerce in 1842, and tea shipments began in 1853. Foreign houses deal mainly in opium and tea, while native merchants trade timber, paper, cloth, and fruit. Imports ran near 1.4 million pounds in 1904 against exports of about one million.
britannica-1911-glasgow:
Glasgow is a city, royal burgh and port of Lanarkshire, Scotland, standing on both banks of the Clyde. The 1911 Britannica entry places it 47 miles west-south-west of Edinburgh. The commercial centre and most great public buildings lie on the north bank, and the article walks the river bridge by bridge.

As a full city article it then works through Glasgow in order. It covers the cathedral, which survives in excellent preservation, the university and public buildings. Docks and shipbuilding, trade and population follow. So does the city's history from its early church endowments. The Clyde, closely held by hills, gives the city an irregular, picturesque site, and the entry keeps returning to the river as the source of Glasgow's trade and growth. It is one of the longest Scottish city articles in the volume, written for a reader who wants the whole city, not a summary.
britannica-1911-jarrow:
Jarrow is a port and borough in the Jarrow division of Durham, England. It stands on the right bank of the Tyne, six and a half miles below Newcastle, on a branch of the North-Eastern railway. Its people numbered 34,295 in 1901. The parish church of St Paul was founded in 685 and keeps parts of work from before the Norman age. Its central tower is Norman, with later details in the Decorated and Perpendicular styles.

Beside the church lie the ruins of the monastery begun by Biscop in 681 and consecrated by Ceolfrid in 685. The Venerable Bede spent his life there, and pilgrims visited his tomb until it was moved to Durham. The town itself is wholly industrial, built on shipbuilding, chemical works, paper mills, and the nearby collieries, and it ships a great quantity of coal from the docks on Jarrow Slake.
britannica-1911-jaworow:
Jaworow is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town in Galicia, Austria, west of Lemberg. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred as just over ten thousand. Local works included a pottery, a brewery, and a distillery, with some trade in farm produce.

Near the town lay a watering place with sulphur springs, the entry notes. The town was a favourite residence of John Sobieski. There he received praise from the pope and from Venice for his victory over the Turks at Vienna. At Jaworow, Peter the Great was betrothed to Catherine, the entry adds.
britannica-1911-linlithgow:
Linlithgow, a royal burgh and county town of Linlithgowshire in Scotland, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its count in 1901 was 4,279 souls in the burgh. It lies in a valley on the south side of a loch, about 17 miles west of Edinburgh by rail. For long it kept an antique, pleasing look, with gardens running down to the lake.

Much of the town was rebuilt in the 1800s, the text notes. Four miles south lies Torphichen, where the Knights of Saint John had their chief Scottish house. The parish kirk stands on the site of the nave of the old church of that order. Ruins of the transept and part of the choir still exist beside it. Trades in Linlithgow are shoe making, tanning, paper, glue, soap, and distilling. The burgh votes with the Falkirk group of towns for parliament.
britannica-1911-lucknow:
Lucknow is the subject of a city entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It covers a city, district, and division of British India. The city was the capital of Oudh from seventeen seventy five until it merged into the United Provinces. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred one as over two hundred sixty thousand.

It lies mainly on the right bank of the winding Gumti river. Two rail bridges and three road bridges cross that river. Colleges named include Canning College and La Martiniere, the latter backed by an endowment from a general. Local crafts in brocade, muslin, brass, and pottery are also listed.
britannica-1911-marlow:
Marlow is a market town in Buckinghamshire, England, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its Thames setting. It stands on the north bank of the river, held close between low wooded hills, with 4,526 people in its urban district in 1901. A weir and lock sit near the tall tower and spire of All Saints church.

The entry calls the town a favorite resort for boating and fishing, mostly modern in look but with some old houses. One house was occupied by the poet Shelley in 1817. Its trades include chairs, lace, paper, and beer. The town appears as a manor in Domesday Book, and its importance likely came from the bridge over the Thames.
britannica-1911-padstow:
Padstow is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a small seaport in Cornwall, England. It is also a market town of that county. It lies in the Saint Austell parliamentary division. A branch of a southern railway serves the town. A count from 1901 gives the urban district 1566 people. It lies near the north coast on the west shore. The estuary of the river Camel opens near by.

That inlet runs six miles into the land from Padstow Bay. The church of Saint Petrock is the town's chief building. A massive roodstone stands in its churchyard. The church is mainly Perpendicular in style. Its tower is of the earlier English style. Inside are an ancient font and a canopied piscina. A fine timber roof spans the nave and aisles. Other old churches of note stand in the locality. Saint Enodock's, long buried in sand drifts, is the most remarkable.
britannica-1911-port-glasgow:
Port Glasgow is a port town of Renfrewshire in Scotland, on the Firth of Clyde. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 16,857 people in 1901. Hills behind the town rise to 700 feet, dotted with villas. The town house of 1815 has a tower and spire. Ship yards and foundries drive the work of the port. Its docks span 16 acres, with 2,000 yards of quay.

The ground can be reached by ships at all tides. The town began as the village of Newark in Kilmalcolm parish. Glasgow's rulers bought it in 1668 and built a harbour there. In 1710 it became the chief customs port for the Clyde. Greenock later took that rank from it. Its graving dock of 1762 was the first of its kind in Scotland. The ruins of Newark Castle stand just east of the town.
britannica-1911-su-chow:
Su Chow is a name borne by three towns in China in this 1911 Britannica place entry. The great one lies in Kiang su on the Grand Canal, west of Shanghai. It stands on a cluster of isles by Lake Tai hu. Walls ten miles round guard the town and its four large outskirts. Silk goods of more kinds are made there than in any town of the realm.

Cheap prints of the old Chinese books are a famed craft of the place. A nine floor pagoda at its north shrine ranks with the best in the land. War left it in ruins in the early sixties, but silk looms and rice trade brought it back. Two more towns of the name get short notes, one a rhubarb mart by the Great Wall.
britannica-1911-tallow:
Tallow, the hard fat of cattle and sheep, is the topic of a trade entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The head word is traced to old forms in Dutch and Low German. In trade the fat comes almost all from oxen and sheep.
