Ox tallow is a hard fat with a pale yellow white hue at room heat. It will not melt in cold spirits, but it does melt in hot spirits and in some oils. Food, age, and health of the beast change how hard it is and when it melts. New tallow melts at a heat a bit above blood heat. Mutton tallow is whiter and harder, with less of the liquid fat olein.
britannica-1911-tow: Tow is a term in textile making for short fibres, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. Such fibres are formed in the processes of scutching and hackling of flax. The word is also used for the yarns made from those short fibres. A machine called a tow card forms the fibres into a sliver. That sliver then passes to the drawing frames, and from there it follows the same process as line yarns in flax spinning.
britannica-1911-walthamstow:
Walthamstow is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a fast growing suburb of London in the county of Essex. The suburb stands east of the river Lea, with rail links into the city. Low hills that once held forest land shelter it on two sides.

The entry gives counts that show the town more than doubled in ten years. It notes the old church, its brass plates, and its schools and art school. Beer making is named as the main trade. A long land history follows the estate from Saxon lords to later great families. Links to a famed diarist and a poet are also noted.
britannica-1911-wuchow:
Wuchow is a treaty port in Kwang si province, China, on the West river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it where the Cassia river joins that stream. It opened to foreign trade in 1897 and links by water to Canton. Trade through its customs topped one and a half million pounds in 1908.

Cotton goods and kerosene led its imports at that time. Sugar, oils, hides, and aniseed led its exports in turn. Summer floods can lift the river fifty feet at the town. Shops and offices thus sit on pontoons tied to the bank. Its site makes it a natural hub between inland provinces and Canton.
bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-giving-a-:
A show planned by two children fills this Laura Lee Hope tale of Bunny Brown and his sister Sue. Grosset and Dunlap put out the book at New York. Snow at the skylight opens the tale. Sue dances in with the news while Bunny eats a late plate of buckwheat cakes and syrup.

Talking it over heads the list of chapters. A climbing boy and a cold small singer join the cast. A General Washington part, scenery work, and a trick by Bunny fill the mid-run. Getting ready and a strange voice raise the stakes. The front plate shows Bunny turning over and over in his act. Home folk, kind help, and a plan worked out by small hands frame the whole. The show gives this book its spine, from first snow-day thought to full dress night.
castle-craneycrow:
George Barr McCutcheon's Castle Craneycrow, printed at New York in 1902, opens with the taking of Turk. Philip Quentin, a rich young American, had caught the little burglar in his rooms at night. Instead of the police, he fed him supper and hired him. Turk — Turkington, or James — has served him faithfully for seven years.

Quentin travels to Florence, where Dorothy Garrison, an American heiress, is promised to an Italian prince. Quentin loves her, and the prince's mountain stronghold, Castle Craneycrow, gives the romance its Gothic machinery. An abduction, a siege of suitors, and Turk's underworld talents drive the plot. McCutcheon followed Graustark with this Italian companion piece, trading his invented kingdom for a real duchy's intrigues. The tone is lighter than the peril: a comedy of love against a castle wall, with a burglar as best man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cracow:
A diocesan entry presents Cracow, the prince-bishopric covering western Galicia, bordering Russian Poland, Prussia, and Hungary. Already in existence by the year 1000, its founding is disputed: some argue for King Mieceslaw I in 984, while most place it at 1000 or just before.

Five lists of bishops survive, the oldest from about 1266, though names before Bishop Aaron are unreliable after Bohemian invaders destroyed records in 1039. Three bishops are publicly venerated, above all St. Stanislaus, martyred by King Boleslaw and canonized in 1253. The entry closes with the diocese in music history, as birthplace of the violin makers Amati, Guarneri, and Stradivari.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-wil:
Friedrich Wilhelm Schadow, a Berlin painter born in 1789, led the Düsseldorf Academy to fame in the nineteenth century. Son of the sculptor Johann Gottfried Schadow, he joined the circle around Overbeck at Rome and there became a Catholic. He taught at Berlin from 1819, then moved to Düsseldorf in 1826 as academy director, with many pupils following him.

Schadow prized realism, color, and sober restraint, grounded in strict drawing from plaster casts before nature. He favored oil painting and modest subjects over grand frescoes: devotional scenes, portraits, landscapes, and genre pieces. His Wise and Foolish Virgins, his Four Evangelists, and his Paradise, Purgatory, and Hell show a graceful talent that valued poetic thought above bold form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glasgow:
Glasgow is an archdiocese in the southwest of Scotland, covering Lanark, Dumbarton, and Renfrew, part of Ayrshire, Baldernock in Stirlingshire, and the Cumbrae Isles. Saint Kentigern, or Mungo, founded the see between 540 and 560 and died in 601. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a see restored under Saint David after centuries without regular succession.

Kentigern built a religious community on the Welsh model to preserve the faith among the surrounding Christians. The restored see's first bishop, John Eochy, held it from 1115 to 1147. Twenty-three successors followed in actual possession until 1560, when Parliament abolished the Catholic faith. Its bishops served as chancellors, treasurers, and regents, and William Turnbull won the charter for the University of Glasgow in 1450.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jakob-benignu:
Physician and anatomist Jakob Benignus Winslow was born at Odense, Denmark, on 27 April 1669. He died at Paris on 3 April 1760. He finished high school at Odense in 1687. He then attended Copenhagen university, studying philosophy and theology. Later he chose medicine and earned a bachelor's degree in 1694. On a royal scholarship he went abroad for training in 1697. He reached Paris in spring 1698.

There he met the Catholic religion. A thorough study of controverted questions, begun to strengthen his Lutheran faith, brought him into the Church instead. Bossuet himself received his profession of faith on 8 October 1699. Conversion made return to Denmark impossible. Despite money troubles, he continued medical studies under Duverney. In autumn 1704 he received his licentiate degree free of charge. The entry presents a convert anatomist of Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-barrow:
John Barrow was a Lancashire priest of notable courage who served the Claughton mission for forty-five years. Born at Westby-in-the-Fylde in 1735 to stout Catholic yeomen, he spent seven years studying at the English College in Rome. Pressed into service at Portsmouth, he spent five years in the navy. He then deserted at Dunkirk and talked his way past a court-martial by pretending to know only Italian.

Ordained at Douai in 1766, he rode to Claughton that July and stayed until his death in 1811. Master of French and Italian, writer of elegant Latin and forceful English, he enlarged the parish church. He improved roads as township overseer, reinvested clergy funds wisely, and negotiated the land for Ushaw College. Though he sometimes slighted his own bishop's wishes, he demanded obedience to Church authority from everyone else, and Rome praised his loyalty and zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-of-cr:
A scholar, preacher, and envoy, Matthew of Cracow was born about 1335 and died at Pisa in 1410. The old tale of noble Pomeranian blood is now discredited; his father was likely a notary at Cracow. He took degrees at Prague, served as dean there, and by 1387 appears as a professor of theology and city preacher. In 1395 he moved to Heidelberg, became rector a year later, and counselled the ruler Ruprecht II.

Ruprecht III's rise as King of Rome in 1400 opened a statesman's career. It brought embassies and court missions, including a plea at Rome in 1403 and greetings to Innocent VII in 1404. Named Bishop of Worms that year, he kept teaching at Heidelberg and declined a cardinal's hat. His writings span Bible commentaries, sermons, and works on confession, conscience, the Eucharist, and the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-of-ja:
Matthew of Janow, a Bohemian church writer of the fourteenth century, died at Prague in 1394. Son of the knight Wenzel of Janow, he studied at Prague and Paris, earning the title Parisian Master after nine years abroad. In 1381 he became canon and confessor at Prague Cathedral, posts he held for life, and he won note less for preaching than for zeal in the confessional.

Between 1388 and 1392 he gathered his treatises as the Regulae Veteris et Novi Testamenti, a work never printed whole and nowhere surviving complete. Parts were wrongly printed among Hus's writings. Blaming the Papal Schism and abuses around exemptions, relics, and images, he urged daily Communion for lay folk. He also urged the removal of images from churches, views the Prague synod of 1389 rejected. He later retracted, and the entry insists he was no forerunner of Hus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moscow:
Moscow, Russian Moskva, was Russia's ancient capital and chief city of its province. It stands near the centre of European Russia on both banks of the river that gives it its name. Fourth capital after Novgorod, Kiev and Vladimir, it housed the tsars from 1340 until Peter the Great moved the court in 1711. Poets call it Bielokamennaya, the White-Walled.

Its population reached 1,335,104 by 1907, making it Russia's greatest commercial and industrial city. It held 440 churches, 24 convents, over 500 schools including the university, some 502 charitable establishments and 23 cemeteries. The entry divides the city grown around the Kremlin into five concentric parts. It follows its churches, monasteries, Catholic parishes and history from foundation to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-t:
Our Lady of the Snow is a feast kept on 5 August to mark the dedication of Santa Maria Maggiore on Rome's Esquiline Hill. Pope Liberius built the first church there between 352 and 366, and it bore his name, Basilica Liberii. Pope Sixtus III restored it between 432 and 440 and dedicated it to Our Lady, and from the seventh century it also bore the name Mary at the Manger.

The name of the snow, and the legend behind it, came a few hundred years later. The tale tells how the childless patrician John and his wife vowed their wealth to Our Lady. They prayed to learn how to spend it, and woke on 5 August to snow on the Esquiline summit. Following a vision of the same night, they built a basilica on the snow-covered spot. No mention of the marvel appears until centuries later, not even in Sixtus's own dedication lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-brist:
Richard Bristow was born at Worcester in 1538 and died at Harrow-on-the-Hill in 1581. Oxford took him in 1555, likely to Exeter College, though Wood doubts the college link. He took his bachelor's degree in 1559 and proceeded Master of Arts at Christ Church in 1562. Exceptionally brilliant and eloquent, he was esteemed as an orator so highly that, with Edmund Campion, he was chosen to dispute publicly before Queen Elizabeth in 1566.

Soon after, having turned to theology and won a wide name for learning, he became a Fellow of Exeter College in 1567 through Sir William Petre, founder of several fellowships there. His ability would probably have won him further promotion, but his religious opinions changed, as an argument with the Regius Professor already showed. The entry follows a scholar whose changing opinions checked a rising Oxford career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rose-window:
A rose window is a round window whose mullions and tracery spread out from the centre, filled with stained glass. The name comes from its fancied resemblance to a rose and its petals. It is one of the most beautiful features of medieval architecture, especially French Gothic. Its origin lies in the Roman oculus, which became a window in the Romanesque period.

By the mid-thirteenth century it had reached its greatest size, the entire width of the nave. Its splendour lasted in France until later fourteenth- and fifteenth-century misfortunes halted large church building. The finest examples stand in the Ile de France and nearby Picardy and Champagne, including Mantes about 1200 and Notre Dame of Paris about 1220. Later steps put the rose under a pointed arch, as at Reims in 1230, then inscribed it in a square, as in the Paris transepts of 1257.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-dur:
Durrow, Irish Dairmagh, Plain of the Oaks, lies delightfully in King's County a few miles from Tullamore. Columba, who loved building near oak groves for their beauty and to strip them of druidic associations, found here, as at Derry, a site after his heart. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a monastery through exile and succession quarrels.

Aedh, son of Brendan, lord of the soil, freely gave the site in 553, and Columba founded his monastery, ruling it with more or less steady care until 563. That year, whether in penance or, as Adamnan says, by choice for Christ's sake, he sailed into Scottish exile. He named Cormac Ua Liathain to succeed him, but tribal jealousies between north and south drove Cormac out, leaving Columba's cousin Laisren in charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-margaret-c:
Margaret Clitherow, Pearl of York, was pressed to death for harbouring priests and refusing to plead. Born about 1556 to Thomas Middleton, York's sheriff in 1564 and 1565 and a wax-chandler, she married John Clitherow, a wealthy butcher and city chamberlain, at St. Martin's, Coney Street, on 8 July 1571. They lived in the Shambles. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 25 March 1586.

Converted about three years later, she grew fervent, risking life by harbouring and maintaining priests. She endured frequent imprisonment, sometimes for two years, yet never daunted. Though her husband was of the Established Church, his brother was a priest. Margaret kept two hiding chambers, one adjoining her house and one elsewhere in the city, with Mass celebrated continually through persecution's thickest years. Some of her priests died martyrs, and Margaret, longing for the same grace, made secret night pilgrimages to York Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stanislaus:
Stanislaus of Cracow, bishop and martyr, is patron of Poland and its ancient capital. Born at Szczepanów on 26 July 1030 to the pious nobles Belislaus and Bogna, he studied at Gniezno and perhaps Paris. After his parents died he gave his ample inheritance to the poor. Bishop Lambert Zula ordained him, made him pastor, canon, cathedral preacher, and vicar-general.

On Lambert's death he was elected bishop, accepting only on Pope Alexander II's explicit command. He worked with energy for reform, but clashed with King Boleslaus II, whom he excommunicated for cruelty and injustice. The king struck him down, tradition says at Mass, on 8 May 1079. No contemporary life survives, and his canonisation life mixes legend with history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislawow:
Stanislawów, a diocese of the Greek-Ruthenian rite in Galicia, served nearly a million faithful under Austria. Its establishment was decided in May 1850 but took effect only with the brief De universo dominico grege of 26 March 1885 and imperial decrees that December. Suffragan of Lwów, it covered most of south-eastern Galicia and all Bukovina as far as Halicz.

It counted twenty-one deaneries and sixty-three chapels. It held 433 churches with resident priests and 298 without. Its clergy numbered 579 secular and thirteen regular priests. It also held four Reformed Basilian monasteries, two Basilian convents, and ten convents of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin. Greek-Ruthenian Catholics numbered 920,000 of a population of 1,387,930, beside Armenians and Latins. A seminary opened in 1907, after clergy trained at Lwów and Vienna. Its town was founded by Stanislav Potocki, dead in 1683.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarnow:
Tarnow is a diocese of western Galicia in Austria. Posen, founded in 968 by Duke Miecyslaw, stood alone in Poland until 1100. That year Otto III and Duke Boleslaw founded Gnesen and Cracow, to which western Galicia then belonged. In the First Partition of 1772 that land fell to Austria. It was cut from foreign Cracow and run from Tarnow by vicar-general Johann von Duval. He became first bishop when the see was erected in 1783.

After the Third Partition of 1795 brought Cracow to Austria too, the see was split. On the second bishop's death in 1801 it was divided between Cracow and Przemysl. Vienna's peace of 1809 handed western Galicia to the Duchy of Warsaw, and Tarnow fell under Lemberg. The Congress of Vienna restored Galicia to Austria. Francis then gave Tarnow a new bishop in 1822, Gregorius Thomas Ziegler, who settled at Tarnow in 1826 after stops at Tyniec and Bochnia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-universit:
Poland's university at Cracow, planned by Casimir the Great, is traced here from first documents to full faculties. Evidence for the scheme dates from 1362, Urban V favoured it, and Casimir chartered the university on 12 May 1364, modelled on Padua and Bologna, with law and Roman law first. Papal approval of 1 September 1364 excluded theology.

Jagiello and Hedwig of Anjou refounded the school. Boniface IX consented on 11 February 1397, and Jagiello signed a new charter on 26 July 1400, now with all four faculties on the Paris pattern. Bishop Peter Wysz, first chancellor, gave the opening lecture. Bohemian, German, and Polish professors, trained mostly at Prague, taught 205 students in year one, rising to 500.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edward-am:
Edward Ambrose Barlow, alias Radcliffe and Brereton, was a priest and martyr born at Barlow Hall in 1585, who died on 10 September 1641. Fourth son of Sir Alexander Barlow of Barlow Hall near Manchester and Mary Brereton of Handforth Hall, he was baptized at Didsbury Church on 30 November 1585. The register entry may still be seen. Schooled at the Benedictine monastery of St Gregory, Douai, he entered the English College at Valladolid in 1610.

He returned to Douai, where his elder brother William Rudesind was a professed monk, was professed himself in 1616, and ordained in 1617. Sent to England, he laboured in south Lancashire with apostolic zeal, living chiefly at Wardley Hall and Morley's Hall. Arrested in 1641, he was condemned for his priesthood and suffered at Lancaster, steadfast to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-fing: F. M. Rudge's Catholic Encyclopedia entry records John Finglow, an English martyr born at Barnby near Howden in Yorkshire. Ordained priest at the English College, Reims, on 25 March 1581, he was sent on the English mission the following month and laboured in the north. Seized and held in Ousebridge Kidcote at York, he was tried as a Catholic priest for reconciling subjects to the old faith, then hanged, drawn and quartered on 8 August 1586.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-peter-sno: John Wainewright's Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces Peter Snow, an English martyr born at or near Ripon. He arrived at the English College, Reims, in April 1589, took tonsure and minor orders in 1590, and was ordained deacon and priest at Soissons in March 1591. He left for England that May. Arrested about 1 May 1598 on his way to York with Ralph Grimston of Nidd, Snow was condemned for treason as a priest and suffered at York on 15 June 1598.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-b:
William Barrow, alias Waring or Harcourt, was an English Jesuit executed at Tyburn in June 1679. Born in Lancashire in 1609, he studied at St-Omer, entered the Society at Watten in 1632, and worked the London district for thirty-five years, becoming its superior early in 1678.

That May he was arrested and sent to Newgate on charges linked to the alleged Popish Plot. His trial with fellow Jesuits Thomas Whitbread, John Fenwick, John Gavan, and Anthony Turner became infamous. Chief Justice Scroggs ruled that the accusers' recent royal pardons barred any mention of their past misdeeds, and that no Catholic witness could be believed. Though the prisoners exposed wholesale perjury by Oates, Bedloe, and Dugdale, they were condemned for high treason and suffered together at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-widow:
Widow is treated here through canonical prescriptions, above all in the Old Testament, where remarriage law dominates. The high priest might not marry a widow, while other priests might marry a fellow priest's widow but not a layman's.

Outside those rules no Old Testament law restricted a widow's remarriage. Support for widows was commended to Israelite charity: they received gleanings of cornfields, olive trees. Vineyards, a share in the third year's tithe, and invitations to feast with the nearest householder at the three principal solemnities. In Maccabean times money and provisions were kept in Jerusalem's Temple for widows' subsistence, and battle spoils were shared with them. For their protection the law forbade taking a widow's garment in pawn, and Job counts seizing a widow's ox for a pledge a wicked act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-rudes:
William Rudesind Barlow was an English Benedictine scholar counted the chief schoolman of his age. His birth date is uncertain; he died at Douai on 19 September 1656. Third son of Sir Alexander Barlow of Barlow Hall, he was schooled with his younger brother, the martyr Edward Barlow, at Douai. Wishing to become a Benedictine, he professed with the Spanish congregation at Cella Nueva in Galicia in 1605 and took his doctorate at Salamanca.

Ordained in 1608, Barlow became prior of Saint Gregory's, Douai, in 1614 and taught theology at Saint Vaast's for forty years, shaping nearly all the bishops, abbots, and teachers of those parts. Weldon calls him first among scholastic divines and casuists, inferior to none in canon law. He refused abbacies and bishoprics, led the English Congregation as president-general from 1621 to 1629, and left almost no writings, his papers destroyed by an enemy after his death.
crome-yellow:
Aldous Huxley's first novel, Crome Yellow, opens on a slow train through Bole, Tritton, and Spavin Delawarr, stations Denis Stone knows by heart. Denis, a young poet, travels to Crome, the country house of Henry Wimbush, for a weekend of artists and talkers. He piles his chattels neatly in the corner, in the futile way the narrator mocks at once.

The house party includes the deaf Anne and the painter Gombauld. The historian host reads his county history aloud. Prophets of the future like Mr Scogan compare Caesars to queen bees raised by special food. Huxley's satire of Bloomsbury and peacock talk made his name in 1921. Denis's failed romance keeps the wit humane.
dark-hollow:
Anna Katharine Green's Dark Hollow, published by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1914, begins with a gate standing ajar. Judge Ostrander's house in Shelby has opened its doors to no outsider for over a dozen years. A group of neighbours gathers, eager and hesitating, before the fence. The woman in purple has been seen at the gate.

Books one to three unwind the judge's buried secret: a man killed years ago, a servant named Bela, and a wife who vanished. Deborah Scranton, a widow of courage, forces the gates from outside. Courtroom scenes, a bit of steel, and unwelcome truths prepare the vigil at Tempest Lodge. Green, a founder of the detective novel, builds her mystery on character and conscience. The curtain lifts at last on Dark Hollow itself, in a sunset of expiation.
doe-osti-3021347-collaborative-fundament:
University of Florida final technical report by David Hibbitts for DOE Basic Energy Sciences award DE-SC0025029. It covers a short reporting period, September 1 to December 31, 2024, on water's role in zeolite catalysis. Zeolites are porous crystals whose aluminum sites do the chemistry; where those sites sit inside the MFI framework, channel or intersection, changes what reactions do. The project, part of a joint effort on the circular carbon economy, used density functional theory as its main tool.

The math mapped how structure-directing agents bias aluminum, gallium, iron, and boron into distinct framework positions, through electrostatics, hydrogen bonding, and confinement. Other runs traced toluene methylation pathways with methanol and dimethyl ether, showing how confinement reshapes transition states and product selectivity. The report notes the project continued under a new award at Purdue University after the lead investigator moved.
doe-osti-3024210-pumped-thermal-energy-s:
Zhiwen Ma, Josh McTigue, Jeffrey Gifford, and six colleagues at the National Laboratory of the Rockies report a pumped thermal energy storage design in NLR/TP-5700-98019, dated March 2026. Pumped thermal storage banks energy as heat in cheap particles, then runs the heat back through a power cycle. A fluid bed heat exchanger is the project's chosen path to strong power efficiency.

Testing exposed a touchy control problem. The mixed bed ran at an average air flow of 24.2 standard cubic feet per minute and the fluidized bed at 24.9, a difference of only 0.4 grams of air per second. Small flow wobbles can tip the bed into fluidization, and once tripped it does not recover easily, since mixing raises temperatures through the whole column. Much effort went into controls that hold the flow steady.
doe-osti-3624639-a-multiomics-mass-spect: Pacific Northwest report PNNL-39684, dated August 2026, is a single abstract page, not a full study. Aivett Bilbao is the named author, and Agilent Technologies is the partner under CRADA 726. The abstract describes work with the Agile Biofoundry, a multi-lab group that speeds bioproducts to market. PNNL and Agilent are building a prototype system that runs hundreds of samples per day. It pairs liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry with artificial intelligence software. The aim is fast, broad strain improvement across metabolomics, lipidomics, and proteomics measures.
doe-osti-3912522-frequency-extraction-fr:
Brookhaven technical note NSLSII-ASD-TN-452, dated August 12, 2026, offers a geometric way to read the rhythms of orderly motion. Four authors are printed: Derong Xu, Yongjun Li, Yue Hao, and Sergei Nagaitsev. In integrable systems, motion winds around invariant tori, each carrying base frequencies. Standard routes to those numbers need action-angle variables or long tracked trajectories. The invariant-flow method takes a shorter path.

The conserved quantities themselves generate flows that commute with one another. Timing a trip along those flows yields the frequencies directly. A small integer matrix links the winding pattern to the timing results. Once set for one torus, that matrix serves its neighbours. The procedure is an explicit algorithm for systems with several degrees of freedom. A test on the McMillan map reached high accuracy. The framing also suits near-integrable machines.
fairy-tales-every-child-should-know:
Mabie's Fairy Tales Every Child Should Know gathers classic tales for young readers. Hamilton Wright Mabie edited the volume for the What-Every-Child-Should-Know Library. The title page is dated 1905. Tales come from Grimm, Perrault, the Arabian Nights, and Madame d'Aulnoy.

Grimm pieces include Hansel and Grethel and The Golden Goose. Aladdin, Ali Baba, and Sindbad's second voyage represent the Arabian Nights. The White Cat and The Fair One with the Golden Locks come from d'Aulnoy. Perrault gives Blue Beard, Cinderella, and Puss in Boots. Tom Thumb traces to Richard Johnson's 1621 prose version, the notes say. Mabie shapes a starter canon of wonder tales for children.
famous-stories-every-child-should-know:
Mabie's Famous Stories Every Child Should Know offers eleven longer tales for young readers. Hamilton Wright Mabie edited it for the What-Every-Child-Should-Know Library. The copyright page is dated 1907. Each story is complete in itself, by a named author.

Dickens opens with A Child's Dream of a Star. Ruskin's King of the Golden River follows as the second piece. Hawthorne gives The Snow Image and The Great Stone Face. Fouqué's Undine and the Book of Ruth stand between them. Cowper's John Gilpin adds comic verse in prose company. Hale's The Man Without a Country supplies the patriotic tale. Ouida's Nürnberg Stove, John Brown's Rab and His Friends, and Austin's Peter Rugg close the set.
fern-s-hollow:
Stretton writes for the young in Fern's Hollow, a tale of a collier's family printed in 1864. Hesba Stretton sets the story at Botfield, a mining village. Her hero is Stephen Fern, whose father lies dying in a hut in the hollow as the tale opens. The chapter heads map his road: homeless days, a cabin on the cinder-hill, and a master's deathbed.

Work and faith test the family page by page. Stephen meets the gamekeeper, speaks his testimony, and learns forgiveness. His sister Martha takes work with a washerwoman at ninepence a day, with little Nan at her side. Collier lads admire Martha as the neatest lass in Botfield. The book joins plain village life to a strong moral thread, in the manner that made Stretton a famed name in homes.
flame-and-shadow:
Sara Teasdale's Flame and Shadow, published after Love Songs made her famous, groups its lyrics in five numbered sections. Early poems like Blue Squills, Stars, and I Have Loved Hours at Sea set her themes: nature watched closely, love gained and lost, and time passing. A French motto about receiving flame or shadow opens the book.

Later sections move through places, day and night, pain, and spring torrents, with titles such as In a Hospital, The Broken Field, and If I Must Go. Teasdale's diction stays plain while her images sharpen, a leaf or a lizard carrying whole moods. The collection won admirers for its music and restraint, and it shows her art at full maturity.
flight-from-tomorrow:
Piper sends a tyrant fleeing through time in Flight From Tomorrow, a complete novelette. H. Beam Piper opens on the fall of Hradzka. Yesterday a whole planet shouted Hail Hradzka. Today the crowds scream for the tyrant's death, and his palace is an inferno of heat-beams and rebels.

Hunted and hated in two worlds, Hradzka takes refuge in the past, with his knowledge of the future as his one wealth. The sampled pages find him hiding in ravines near a farm, sure at last that no one follows. He comes on the stream and pool where he slept the night he arrived. The young pines there, green then, stand blighted now, their needles brown. Piper lets that small change carry the chill of the tale: the past is not quite the place the fugitive thought he knew.
folk-tales-every-child-should-know:
Mabie chooses the world's tales for the young in Folk Tales Every Child Should Know. Hamilton Wright Mabie edited the volume for a library of books every child should know. Its tales come from many lands and many tellers. Dasent gives Why the Sea is Salt and the lad who went to the North Wind. Mitford gives the grateful foxes of Japan.

Lal Behari Day gives the origin of rubies, and George Bird Grinnell the dun horse. Balzac's peasant story of Napoleon and Joel Chandler Harris on Brother Bear stand in the same covers. The sampled pages send a shepherd to a lake to call out a dragon. He sets his falcon on a stump, his hounds and bagpipes by, and wades in with a shout, while the emperor's grooms watch from a hill. The book is a world tour of the fireside tale.
from-a-college-window:
Arthur Christopher Benson published From a College Window in 1906, gathering essays from the Cornhill Magazine. Benson, a fellow of Magdalene College at Cambridge, begins with the point of view. Sincerity, he argues, gives any work of art its value. Charm cannot be manufactured, but an honest outlook can be chosen.

Eighteen papers follow on growing older, books, conversation, and sociability. Beauty, art, egotism, and education each receive a quiet hearing. Ambition and the simple life are weighed against each other. Games, spiritualism, habits, and religion close the set. Benson writes from his window in a level, confiding voice. The essays made him the best-loved English essayist of his generation, a don thinking aloud for readers who wanted reflection without system.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ex:
On September 15, 1970, President Richard Nixon met in the Oval Office for twenty minutes with his advisers. In that short meeting, from 3:25 to 3:45 in the afternoon, he ordered the CIA to push for a military coup in Chile. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, posted fifty years later in September 2020.

The target was Salvador Allende, Chile's newly elected socialist president, before he could take office. The declassified records behind the posting trace how that order set covert action in motion. It is a compact, dated record of the moment the United States chose the most extreme option against an elected government.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
Nearly half a century after General Augusto Pinochet seized power in Chile, key American records about the coup were still secret. This briefing book asks the classic question in its title: what did President Richard Nixon know, and when did he know it?

Its point is the gap itself. Presidential and CIA documents from 1973 remained withheld forty-nine years after the putsch, long after most of the main facts were public. For readers, the posting is evidence of how long intelligence files can stay locked even when the history around them is well known.
heather-and-snow:
George MacDonald set this novel in rural Scotland, among farms, moors, and small villages. Kirsty grows up near the hills with her father David. Francis Gordon, the laird's son, drifts between duty and ease. Steenie, a simple and loyal friend, stands near the heart of the tale.

The chapters trace love, pride, and hard weather across many years. A storm, a race with death, and old family wounds shape the end. MacDonald uses Scots speech and plain faith in daily talk. Readers meet a slow, warm story where character matters more than wealth or rank.
heroes-every-child-should-know:
Hamilton Wright Mabie's Heroes Every Child Should Know retells the great hero tales for young readers, in the series Mabie edited for American children. Perseus with his mirrored shield, Theseus, and Hercules open the classical muster. Siegfried comes out of the northern forests, Roland out of France's song, and Arthur out of Britain's. The tales are told straight, the wonder kept and the gore softened. Each hero stands for a kind of courage: strength, loyalty, or dying at a pass for other people.

Mabie, a popular essayist and editor, believed children should meet the heroes before they meet the critics. His prose aims at the fireside: clear, warm, and just formal enough to feel like legend. Readers get the standard American nursery of heroes here, through which generations first learned why Roland blew his horn too late.
his-last-bow:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathered these Sherlock Holmes tales in 1917. Eight stories make up the set, told as ever by Dr Watson. The first opens on a bleak March day in 1892. Holmes gets a telegram at lunch and turns to the word grotesque.

Cases include stolen naval plans, a devil's foot drug, and a red circle. A dying detective and a missing lady add to the set. The title tale puts Holmes to war service for Britain. Readers get late Holmes in fine form: sharp logic, grim foes, and friendship at the core.
humphrey-bold-a-story-of-the-times-of-be:
Herbert Strang wrote this boys' sea story, published in 1909. Humphrey Bold tells it in the first person. He breaks his indentures, meets the Mohocks, and falls among thieves. Admiral Benbow gives the tale its age and its standard of courage.

Humphrey fights the French captain Duguay-Trouin and wins the king's commission. Prisoners are marched gagged, dressed as French soldiers with bandaged heads, in one ruse. Cables are cut and councils of war held as the war tightens. Dick Cludde and Uncle Moses add rogues and helpers. Strang packs the chapters with escapes and sea fights, in the best school-story manner.
hunting-with-the-bow-arrow:
Saxton Pope wrote this archery and hunting manual, dedicated to Robin Hood. Pope calls Robin a spirit that dwells at some time in every youth's heart. The first chapters tell of Ishi, the last Yana Indian. Ishi's bow, arrows, and hunting methods are set down in detail.

Making bows and arrows follows, then equipment and how to shoot. Raccoon, deer, bear, and mountain lion hunts fill the field chapters. Stewart Edward White adds a chapter of encouragement. Native tales of the coyote doctor season the lore. Pope writes as doctor, craftsman, and hunter at once. The book revived the longbow for a machine age.
lazy-thoughts-of-a-lazy-girl-sister-of-t:
Jenny Wren wrote Lazy Thoughts of a Lazy Girl as a set of light essays. Hurst and Company published it in New York. She bills herself as sister of that Idle Fellow.

Twelve short chapters treat love, bills, politics, and afternoon tea. Dress, Christmas, town, and country each get a chapter. Children, dogs, concerts, and dancing fill the later pages. Her tone is chatty, amused, and deliberately unhurried. The book offers Victorian drawing room humor in small, easy doses. Her laziness is a pose for wit, not true idleness. Each short chapter lands one or two neat social jokes.
little-sister-snow:
Frances Little published this Japan story in 1909. Genjiro Kataoka supplied the illustrations. She dedicates it to her niece Alice Hegan Rice. Happy months spent together in Japan inspired the dedication.

Its heroine, Yuki San, is called before her father early. She paints, serves tea, and promises the gods faithfully. Two old people and flying feet fill the picture list. Little, author of The Lady of the Decoration, sets childhood in Japan. Yuki busies herself serving tea in one listed illustration. Not willing to be surpassed in salutation, another caption reads.
love-s-shadow:
Love's Shadow, first published in London in 1908, opens Ada Leverson's Little Ottleys series. Its motto comes from Shakespeare: love flies when pursued. The story opens at breakfast in a tiny new Knightsbridge flat. Bruce Ottley begs his wife Edith not to make him late for the office.

Edith is young, pretty, and more subtle than she looks. The flat, exactly like thousands of others, frames their married life. Leverson builds comedy from talk, visits, and small social storms. Hyacinth and other friends draw the young couple into wider circles. The novel is light, sharp, and quietly sad about love. It sets up the Ottley books that follow.
my-lady-ludlow:
Elizabeth Gaskell tells this tale through an old woman's memories. The narrator contrasts slow coach days with fast new trains. Letters once came three times a week, and were read like books. Now short, jerky notes fly in twice a day.

Her father was a poor clergyman with a large family. Her mother kept rank with rich makers by wearing old lace. Lady Ludlow rules the world the narrator recalls. V1 dates the novella to 1858 and links it to Cranford. Gaskell draws the old Tory lady with love and irony, as her world of rank gives way to a new, rougher age.
nasa-tm-19650014499-an-exploratory-inves:
William J Alford Jr and William P Henderson ran low-speed tunnel studies on four aircraft shapes with wings that change sweep. Swing wings fly with wings out for slow flight, then swept back for speed. At low speed, that freedom can hurt stability. The fourth shape was designed using lessons from the first three.

That final shape proved steady in pitch for all sweep angles above twelve and a half degrees. It was also steady in direction across the angles and lift levels tested. Its largest static margin was only about nine and a half percent. The study shows design learning in action, shape by shape.
nasa-tm-19660017786-wave-plan-analysis-o:
Don J Wood, Robert G Dorsch, and Charlene Lightner at Lewis Research Center presented a method for computing unsteady flow in liquid-filled systems, in a paper dated July 12, 1965. Unsteady flow surges and settles rather than running evenly. Their wave-plan method builds the flow from small pressure pulses added together. The model runs on a digital computer and covers the whole system at once.

Viscous resistance and other nonlinear effects are included, the summary says. The analysis fits many kinds of hydraulic systems. A long, straight line serves as their worked example. Sudden surges can burst pipes and valves, so a sound prediction method had value far beyond space work.
nasa-tm-19680010756-optimized-computatio:
R. H. Estes and E. R. Lancaster, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, speed up a classic computing method in March 1968. They apply power series integration to the restricted three-body problem. Their new recursion formulas for the series terms cut computing time sharply compared with earlier authors' versions.

The paper also takes up step size: how far the calculation can leap at once. It discusses and extends Van Flandern's method for getting the most step per unit of computer time. Error control guides the choices throughout. A method for keeping the series terms from ballooning is presented as well.
nasa-tm-19700009885-experimental-perform:
David B. Fenn, James N. Deyo, Thomas J. Miller, and Richard W. Vernon ran this test at the Lewis Research Center. Their report came out in January 1970. It covers a Brayton power system, sized from two to fifteen kilowatts, run inside the Space Power Facility.

The engine ran for over five hundred hours in a vacuum, using krypton gas. It was the first run of the complete system, the authors state. Most parts were flight-type hardware, apart from the heat source and heat sink. The report gives the power the engine made and the efficiency it reached at set turbine temperatures and pressures.
nasa-tm-19700014599-interface-stability-:
Eugene P. Symons of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in April 1970. It studies what happens when liquid flows into an empty tank in weightlessness. The tanks tested were cylinders with rounded, bowl-shaped ends, at first holding no liquid at all.

In orbit, liquid does not settle to the bottom of a tank the way it does on Earth. Symons ran tests in a weightless setting to watch the liquid surface, called the interface. He recorded when the inflow stayed stable and when it broke up. Tank designers needed such results to move fuel safely between tanks in space.
people-you-know:
George Ade's People You Know appeared in 1904, illustrated by John T. McCutcheon and others. In his preface Ade warns that the book contains no new information. It holds plain observations about people who live just around the corner, and only those people, so no reader need take painful offence.

He also confesses a shameless amount of slang, since the fables are written in the colloquial American language seldom seen in print. Titles like The Periodical Souse and What Father Bumped Into at the Culture Factory give the flavour. Ade's fables made him America's favourite humorist of everyday vanity.
podcast-joerogan-L6IonRH1-ow:
Commentator Blaire White tells Rogan about her DMT experience in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. White, known for blunt online commentary, here tells a personal story instead of arguing a position. The drug's short, intense trip is the whole subject.

She describes what she saw and felt, and how the minutes under the drug stayed with her afterward. Rogan, who has chased the same experience, compares notes and asks what she made of the beings users report. The segment is a candid trip report from an unlikely reporter, told straight, with the fear and the wonder both left in.
quill-s-window: Quill's Window is a novel by George Barr McCutcheon, with a frontispiece by C. Allan Gilbert, shown here by its title page and contents alone. The twenty-four chapters promise a country mystery. The Forbidden Rock opens the list. The Story the Old Man Told and Courtney Thane follow. Dowd's Tavern and Alix the Third appear. So do The Face at the Window and The Disappearance of Rosabel Vick. The Thrower of Stones comes near the end. A close At Quill's Window ends the book.
reminiscences-of-captain-gronow:
Captain Rees Howell Gronow, formerly of the Grenadier Guards and M.P. for Stafford, tells anecdotes of the camp, the court, and the clubs in these memoirs. An editor's note warns that his spelling is creative and French phrases abound. The tales are arranged as titled topics, sometimes linked, sometimes not.

The editor calls Gronow an entertaining storyteller who brings the Regency period and the wars with France to life. Gronow published several sets of such memoirs in his lifetime. The record here holds the first part of his memoirs as he issued them, in pieces that move between army life, high society, and club talk at the close of the wars.
roof-and-meadow:
Dallas Lore Sharp, author of A Watcher in the Woods, wrote these nature essays in a school edition from the Century Company of New York, dated 1911. Bruce Horsfall drew the pictures, and Sharp dedicates the book to his mother. The text had appeared in parts under copyrights of 1902 to 1904.

Birds from a City Roof opens the contents, watching wild life from above a city street. The Hunting of the Woodchuck and Three Sermons follow, then The Marsh at length. Calico and the Kittens brings the farmyard in, and The Sparrow Roost and Mux keep the scale small. Racoon Creek, in the book's kept spelling, closes the set of roof and meadow studies.
stories-in-light-and-shadow:
Bret Harte's Stories in Light and Shadow forms Volume 13 of the Argonaut Edition of his works, printed at New York by P. F. Collier and Son. The contents list Unser Karl, Uncle Jim and Uncle Billy, See Yup, The Desborough Connections, Salomy Jane's Kiss, The Man and the Mountain, and The Passing of Enriquez.

Unser Karl opens in a German town where the American consul walks streets that look like stage sets, full of soldiers standing stiff as toys. Harte moves between California mining country and foreign posts, mixing humor with pathos. His tales weigh luck, loyalty, and the masks people wear in new and raw places.
tales-of-wonder-every-child-should-know: Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Archibald Smith shaped Tales of Wonder Every Child Should Know, issued by Doubleday, Doran and Co. for the Parents' Institute, with rights held from 1909. The front pages thank the firms that let the editors reuse tales, naming Joseph Jacobs, The Grateful Crane from William Elliot Griffis, five tales from Old Deccan Days by M. Frere, and three tales from Russian Grandmother's Wonder Tales by L. S. Houghton.
the-allen-house-or-twenty-years-ago-and-:
T. S. Arthur wrote this moral novel, printed at Philadelphia in 1860 under the title The Allen House, or, Twenty Years Ago and Now. Its preface speaks straight to young men and women at the start of adult life. It warns that a wrong first turn can leave a person, twenty years on, looking back on failed hopes.

The opening chapter brings a tired working man home through a day of heavy rain. His wife meets him with dry clothes, slippers, and tea ready. Warm scenes of home life carry the lesson the preface sets out: daily choices, made early, shape whether later years bring honor and peace or regret.
the-autobiography-of-a-quack-and-the-cas:
S. Weir Mitchell placed two tales in one small volume, both first printed without his name in the Atlantic Monthly. His introduction says the quack's life story was recast with large additions. The second tale, about George Dedlow, began as a manuscript he lent to friends and never meant to print.

Readers took Dedlow's case for fact. Money was raised for the supposed sufferer, and visitors went to a Philadelphia hospital to help him. Mitchell notes that spiritualists welcomed the closing incident as proof of their beliefs. The quack tale opens in a hospital ward, told by a sick man facing a grim diagnosis.
the-bishop-s-shadow:
I. T. Thurston wrote a story for young readers, illustrated by M. Eckerson, under a verse about a tree's shadow. Our shadow selves, the verse says, may fall where we can never be. Thurston is also named for Boys of the Central and A Genuine Lady.

Contents open with a lost pocketbook and a girl Nan's new home. An accident brings a boy called Tode to meet a bishop and enter his house. Tode makes a new start, while Theo does shadow work and gets into trouble. Later headings name Theo's new business, Nan finding friends, a strike, and a call to go up higher.
the-case-of-the-pocket-diary-found-in-th:
The Case of the Pocket Diary Found in the Snow, by Grace Isabel Colbron and Augusta Groner, opens with the introduction to Joe Muller that fronts the Muller books. He is a secret service detective of the Imperial Austrian police. He is a genius in his profession. Yet he differs from the famous detectives. He has neither Holmes's impressive authority nor Lecoq's keen brilliancy.

Muller is small, plain, and self-effacing, and the introduction traces that manner to a miscarriage of justice that imprisoned him in his youth and made honest employment impossible for years after. The world's gain came from his misfortune. Thrown on his own talents, he joined the force. Red tape holds his rank near a policeman's. Still, the department knows its treasure. The case itself waits until its detective stands explained.
the-census-in-moscow:
An essay on the Moscow census of 1882, taken from the 1887 Crowell edition of What to Do?, argues that counting people is a science with a moral aim. A census, it holds, is a study of society, and the point of that study is the happiness of the people. Unlike other sciences, it is carried out by two thousand people drawn from the community itself.

Living people, not distant objects, form its subject matter. A nebula can wait and feels nothing, but the poor of Moscow cannot be treated with the same cold distance. The essay pictures a census taker in a night lodging house, politely asking a starving man his trade and name, then writing him down and moving on. That, the writer insists, is wrong: those who meet the poor face to face owe them humane conduct, not mere figures for later laws.
the-children-s-own-longfellow: A Longfellow volume made for children, with pictures, is shown here by its contents and illustration list alone. The poems named include The Wreck of the Hesperus, The Village Blacksmith, Evangeline, parts of Hiawatha, The Building of the Ship, and Paul Revere's Ride.The front matter is all a reader gets in this record.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-henry-wad:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's complete poetical works appear here in a Household Edition, explained in a publisher's note dated Boston, Autumn, 1902, from Houghton Mifflin. The note says the volume holds the original verse he wished kept, and every translation but the Divina Commedia. The poems stand as nearly as possible in chronological order.

The contents open with Voices of the Night, including the Prelude, A Psalm of Life, The Reaper and the Flowers, and Footsteps of Angels. Earlier poems follow, among them An April Day, Autumn Woods in Winter, and Sunrise on the Hills. Ballads and other poems bring The Skeleton in Armor, The Wreck of the Hesperus, The Village Blacksmith, and Excelsior. A section of poems on slavery names The Slave's Dream and The Quadroon Girl.
the-daughter-of-anderson-crow: George Barr McCutcheon, author of Beverly of Graustark and Jane Cable, wrote The Daughter of Anderson Crow, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1907 with pictures by B. Martin Justice. Its contents open with Anderson Crow, Detective, The Pursuit Begins, The Babe on the Doorstep, and The Village Queen. They run on to Rosalie Has Plans of Her Own, a spelling-bee, a case of mistaken identity, and a haunted house. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-dawn-of-a-to-morrow:
Frances Hodgson Burnett opens The Dawn of a To-morrow on a London fog. There are always two ways of looking at a thing, she says. Two ways suffice for fog. Thick and yellow, it can seem gruesome. Or it can seem a cozy enclosure to a man who wakes rested in a healthy body.

Such a man may watch the housemaid build the fire and enjoy the glow. He takes a sort of pleasure in the mystery outside, with its lamp halos and torch flares over coster barrows. The other way differs hugely. A man who gave his name to the house as Antony Dart wakes in a third-story bedroom of a lodging-house in a poor street, and the tale turns to him.
the-eagle-s-shadow: James Branch Cabell's The Eagle's Shadow, dated 1904, opens with a frontispiece named Margaret. A contents list of thirteen bare chapter numbers follows. The book is set in trust for Martha Louise Branch, in hopes it be judged by its patron's merits more than its maker's. No chapter title or story text appears in these pages. Only the title matter and contents list are present here.
the-flight-of-the-shadow: George MacDonald wrote The Flight of the Shadow as a novel told by a young woman. Mrs. Day begins the tale in the contents. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads name Miss Martha Moon. They name an uncle, his room, and first secrets. A mirror, a garden, and figures called Thanatos and Zoe stand in the list. All this points to a tale of family mystery with a ghostly edge. No chapter text follows in the pages given here.
the-golden-scarecrow:
Hugh Walpole wrote The Golden Scarecrow. George H. Doran Company printed it in New York in 1915. A contents list names a prologue on Hugh Seymour. Chapters then center on one child each: Henry Fitzgeorge Strether, Ernest Henry, Angelina, Bim Rochester, Nancy Ross, Barbara Flint, Sarah Trefusis, and Young John Scarlet.

The prologue opens with Hugh Seymour at nine years of age. He was sent from Ceylon to be schooled in England. His parents lived in Ceylon. His kin were mostly abroad. He spent his holidays as a small, pale paying guest. He stayed in houses where other children counted for more. In some houses children counted for nothing. In 1889, 1890, and 1891 he stayed with the Rev. William Lasher. Lasher was vicar of Clinton St. Mary. That lonely start sets the book's interest in how children see the adult world.
the-guinea-stamp-a-tale-of-modern-glasgo: Annie S. Swan wrote The Guinea Stamp, a tale of modern Glasgow. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a publisher's list for a Five Shilling Series. The list names other tales by Swan: The Gates of Eden and Briar and Palm. It names One False Step, by Andrew Stewart, and Sir John's Ward. No page of the tale itself is present. Its story cannot be told from what is here.
the-idle-thoughts-of-an-idle-fellow: Jerome K. Jerome dedicated this little volume at length to a dear and well-beloved friend of his prosperous and evil days. Only the dedication pages are present here. The essays themselves do not appear. The praise unfolds slowly. The friend never tells him his faults. He never wants to borrow money. The household's women treat him coolly. The dog regards him with suspicion. Yet he grows closer daily. The friend, revealed at the end, is his oldest and strongest pipe, companion of his idle hours.
the-iron-furrow:
George C. Shedd wrote this western novel. A. L. Burt Company published it in New York. Doubleday, Page and Company held the copyright, dated 1919 and 1920. Henry A. Botkin drew the frontispiece. Chapter I opens on scenery alone. The Ventisquero Range stretches across the whole view. Its mountains come tall and blue from the north. They seem to march past in procession. They vanish in the remote south.

The frontispiece caption gives the human counterweight. A man's eyes gaze keen from under a hat brim. The brim is drawn forward to his line of vision. Shedd sets iron and furrow against that range. Settlement and stubborn labor drive the tale. Mountain country tests both. The prose keeps the high manner of its day.
the-journal-of-arthur-stirling-the-valle:
Upton Sinclair edited and condensed this journal, subtitled The Valley of the Shadow. An opening sketch explains its history. Arthur Stirling was known to barely a dozen people in his huge city. Sinclair and his wife were his only friends, Sinclair writes. Stirling taught himself through night labor and impossible jobs. He learned five languages. No man of letters Sinclair knew could match his memory for great poetry. He wrote a blank-verse tragedy called The Captive.

The sketch quotes his death notice from the New York Times of June 9, 1902. Suicide in the Hudson River, it reports. Poet and man of genius, it calls him, dead in his twenty-second year. Sinclair describes a tall, dark-haired boy with a wistful look. He once went a week without speaking to a living soul. The journal records that devotion to art.
the-king-s-men-a-tale-of-to-morrow: Robert Grant published this tale of tomorrow under copyright in 1884. A prefatory note names John Boyle O'Reilly, J. S. Dale, and John T. Wheelwright as collaborators. Only the contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The headings sketch a future royalist plot. Ripon House and Richard Lincoln open them. My lady's chamber and Jarley Jawkins's jollities follow. The royalists and a chapter naming King George the Fifth come next. The raising of the flag, the lion's mouth, and the last royalist close the list.
the-legend-of-sleepy-hollow:
Washington Irving presents his famous tale as papers left by Diedrich Knickerbocker. Tarry Town sits by the Tappan Zee on the Hudson, where Dutch sailors once shortened sail and prayed to Saint Nicholas. Two miles away lies a small valley among high hills.

Irving calls that valley one of the quietest places in the world. A brook murmurs through it, and quail whistles or woodpecker taps break the calm. Schoolmaster Ichabod Crane will meet the Headless Horseman there, yet Irving first builds a drowsy Dutch world of farms, ghosts, and rich autumn food.
the-life-of-george-borrow:
Herbert Jenkins compiled his life of George Borrow from unpublished official papers, Borrow works, and correspondence. John Murray issued it in London in 1912. A preface singles out Borrow happiest working years as 1833 to 1840, spent serving the British and Foreign Bible Society abroad.

In Russia, Portugal, and Spain, Borrow poured out a lifetime of energy, Jenkins says. He rose from an unknown hack writer who peddled unsold translations of Welsh and Danish bards. Readers follow a tinker, traveler, and Bible seller whose books on Spain and Gypsy life made his name.
the-long-shadow: B. M. Bower's The Long Shadow carries a 1908 copyright, illustrations by Clarence Rowe, and a dedication to those who have watched the shadow fall upon the range. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel does not appear. The seventeen chapters follow Charming Billy. They take him through a visitor, a fight, Prune Pie and Coon-can, and a man from Michigan. A winter at the Double-Crank ranch follows. Then the titles darken in sequence: The Shadow Falls Lightly, then The Shadow Darkens.
the-mystery-of-mrs-blencarrow:
Mrs. Oliphant's The Mystery of Mrs. Blencarrow, dated 1890, was printed at Chicago by Donohue, Henneberry and Company. Inside, the chapter heading shortens the title to The Mystery of Blencarrow, dropping the Mrs., while the title page keeps the fuller form. Ten chapters are announced before Chapter I, The Blencarrow Household, begins.

The house stands in a small park beside a bright mountain river, somewhere in Cumberland, Westmorland, or North Lancashire; the narrator cheerfully admits the county boundaries confuse her. Built on a slope, its drawing room overlooks diversified country to a distant lake between blue hills. Inside lives a simple, innocent group. Mrs. Blencarrow, a widow of five or six years, had been the most beloved of wives during a dozen years there.
the-mystery-of-the-hasty-arrow:
Anna Katharine Green's The Mystery of the Hasty Arrow is present here only in title page and the first contents of Book I, so the detective story does not appear. Dodd, Mead and Company held the 1917 copyright; the A. L. Burt Company published this printing in New York by arrangement with them. H. R. Ballinger supplied the frontispiece, whose caption warns against endangering a woman's recovery by any show of curiosity.

Book I is headed A Problem of the First Order. Its six listed chapters begin with Let Some One Speak! and In Room B. I Have Something to Show You, A Strategic Move, Three Where Two Should Be, and The Man in the Gallery complete what is shown.
the-pocket-george-borrow:
The Pocket George Borrow gathers passages chosen from the works of George Borrow by Edward Thomas, in the 1912 Chatto and Windus edition. Thomas explains his method in a short note. A reader who has been through Borrow's books once or twice starts dipping into them. He gradually makes an anthology of his own. This pocket selection offers another man's choices, without pretending to completeness or authority.

Borrow, Thomas warns, is not a pithy writer. He is at his worst when sententious, so the passages run longer than usual in the series. Many fine things, above all from Wild Wales, had to be left out for length. A list of Borrow's writings heads the volume. It names Romantic Ballads, Zincali on the gypsies of Spain, The Bible in Spain, Lavengro, Romany Rye, and Wild Wales. The chosen passages shown in the contents come from Zincali and Lavengro.
the-puritan-widow:
An early modern city comedy set in London opens in a garden behind a widow's house, with the household still in mourning after her husband's burial. Lady Plus enters with her daughters Frances and Moll, her brother-in-law Sir Godfrey, and her son Edmond, all dressed for grief.

The cast list promises crowded intrigue. Suitors press toward the widow and both daughters, while a scholar, an old soldier, a highwayman captain, and sheriff's officers fill out the London world. The widow's outburst of sorrow is quickly answered with attempts at comfort, setting a tone that mixes mourning, money, and courtship.
the-second-thoughts-of-an-idle-fellow: Jerome K. Jerome's The Second Thoughts of an Idle Fellow was published by Hurst and Blackett in London in 1899. The title page lists four printings in quick succession. The first came in August 1898, and the fourth in January 1899. The pages shown give title matter and the start of the contents only. The first essay treats the art of making up one's mind. The second turns to the disadvantage of not getting what one wants. Love philtres are promised later.
the-tale-of-old-mr-crow: Old Mr. Crow is one of Arthur Scott Bailey's Tuck-Me-In Tales, dated 1917. This record stops at the title page and list of chapters, so the outlaw crow's schemes remain untold. Seventeen chapters are named, covering a giant scarecrow, a new umbrella, a queer toadstool, a game of checkers, and a race with a train. One heading admits Mr. Crow has a bad memory, and another promises strange buttons on a tight-fitting new coat. The list alone sketches a wily, vain bird forever getting into trouble.
the-way-we-live-now:
Anthony Trollope's Way We Live Now first appeared in twenty monthly parts from February 1874 to September 1875, then in book form from Chapman and Hall in 1875. An editorial note in this edition corrects a long-standing mistake about the forty illustrations. They were once credited to Samuel Luke Fildes, but recent scholarship gives them to Lionel Grimston Fawkes.

Contents chapters open the novel's world: three editors, the Carbury family, the Beargarden club, and Madame Melmotte's ball. A great railway scheme to Vera Cruz follows, with Mr. Fisker's success and Lady Carbury at home. The note also explains where the two halves of the illustration set were sourced for this electronic edition, from Google Books and the Internet Archive.
to-morrow:
Joseph Conrad's story is set in the little seaport of Colebrook, where Captain Hagberd settled under morbid, unreasonable circumstances. Hagberd bought land and built two ugly yellow brick cottages, living in one and letting the other to blind Josiah Carvil, a retired boat-builder and domestic tyrant. A low fence divides their gardens.

Carvil's daughter Bessie dries washing over that fence, and Hagberd mildly protests each time that it rots the wood. He wears sailcloth from head to foot and keeps rank grass on his side. Readers get a Conrad tale of obsession, neighbours, and waiting built from small repeated acts.
undertow:
Kathleen Norris wrote Undertow, printed as volume seven of her collected works. She dedicated it to Margaret Thomas, with a short poem. Chapter one opens on the marriage of Albert Bradley and Anne Polk Barrett, called Nancy. Both families treat the match as a risky adventure. Her uncle Thomas, a quiet old southerner, and his tiny Boston mother agree on little else. Both warn the young pair that they take a grave chance.

Norris gives Nancy a working past before the wedding. She held a paid post with a private group that aided the poor, earning fifteen dollars a week. Seven of those dollars went for board with Mrs. Terhune, a young widow and old family friend. The opening sets up a marriage between two people of gentle birth but small means. It asks how love holds up once money and daily life press in.
what-the-mother-of-a-deaf-child-ought-to: Just the title page, a dedication, and the first contents entries are present here, so John Dutton Wright's guidance does not appear. Wright ran the Wright Oral School for the Deaf in New York City. Stokes printed his book in March 1915. He wrote it, at his wife's urging, so mothers could do everything possible for their deaf children. The listed chapters start with facing the facts. The next asks how a mother should begin her part of the work. A long preface is listed before them.
what-to-do-thoughts-evoked-by-the-census: Only the title page and Isabel F. Hapgood's translator note are present in this record, so Tolstoy's essays themselves are absent. Count Lyof N. Tolstoi wrote What To Do? after taking part in the Moscow census. Crowell printed Hapgood's English version in New York in 1887. Her note says banned books still reached readers through a Geneva firm. Tolstoy's essays moved in Russia as hand-copied sheets, and she marks where the censor cut the text. A twin record carries the same pages.
